cards.quote: Then, the current at time t across the cross-section of the conductor is defined as the value of the ratio of DQ to Dt in the limit of Dt tending to zero, I (t ) ≡ lim ∆Q ∆t →0 ∆t (3.2)

tex.back:
Then, the current at time $t$ across the cross-section of the conductor is defined as the value of the ratio of $\Delta{Q}$ to $\Delta{t}$ in the limit of $\Delta{t}$ tending to zero,
$$I(t) \equiv \lim_{\Delta{t} \to 0} \frac{\Delta{Q}}{\Delta{t}}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of electric current?
cards.back: In SI units, the unit of current is ampere.
cards.quote: In SI units, the unit of current is ampere.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An ampere is defined through ____ of currents that we will study in the following chapter.
cards.back: An ampere is defined through magnetic effects of currents that we will study in the following chapter.
cards.quote: An ampere is defined through magnetic effects of currents that we will study in the following chapter.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Charges in ____ constitute an electric current.
cards.back: Charges in motion constitute an electric current.
cards.quote: Charges in motion constitute an electric current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the typical order of magnitude of currents in domestic appliances?
cards.back: An ampere is typically the order of magnitude of currents in domestic appliances.
cards.quote: An ampere is typically the order of magnitude of currents in domestic appliances.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are conductors?
cards.back: In other materials, notably metals, some of the electrons are practically free to move within the bulk material. These materials, generally called conductors, develop electric currents in them when an electric field is applied.
cards.quote: In other materials, notably metals, some of the electrons are practically free to move within the bulk material. These materials, generally called conductors, develop electric currents in them when an electric field is applied.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If we consider solid conductors, then of course the atoms are tightly bound to each other so that the current is carried by the ____.
cards.back: If we consider solid conductors, then of course the atoms are tightly bound to each other so that the current is carried by the negatively charged electrons.
cards.quote: If we consider solid conductors, then of course the atoms are tightly bound to each other so that the current is carried by the negatively charged electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In which type of conductor can both positive and negative charges move?
cards.back: There are, however, other types of conductors like electrolytic solutions where positive and negative charges both can move.
cards.quote: There are, however, other types of conductors like electrolytic solutions where positive and negative charges both can move.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An electron colliding with an ion emerges with the ____ as before the collision.
cards.back: An electron colliding with an ion emerges with the same speed as before the collision.
cards.quote: An electron colliding with an ion emerges with the same speed as before the collision.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: After an electron collides with a fixed ion, what is the direction of its velocity?
cards.back: the direction of its velocity after the collision is completely random.
cards.quote: However, the direction of its velocity after the collision is completely random.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: With no electric field applied, why is there no net electric current in a conductor?
cards.back: the number of electrons travelling in any direction will be equal to the number of electrons travelling in the opposite direction. So, there will be no net electric current.
cards.quote: the number of electrons travelling in any direction will be equal to the number of electrons travelling in the opposite direction. So, there will be no net electric current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mechanisms, which maintain a steady electric field are ____ that we shall study later in this chapter.
cards.back: Mechanisms, which maintain a steady electric field are cells or batteries that we shall study later in this chapter.
cards.quote: Mechanisms, which maintain a steady electric field are cells or batteries that we shall study later in this chapter.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A basic law regarding flow of currents was discovered by ____ in ____
cards.back: A basic law regarding flow of currents was discovered by G.S. Ohm in 1828
cards.quote: A basic law regarding flow of currents was discovered by G.S. Ohm in 1828

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: Ohm's law relating the potential difference V across a conductor to the current I through it
cards.back:
or, V = R I
where the constant of proportionality R is called the resistance of the conductor.
cards.quote: Then Ohm's law states that VµI or, V = R I (3.3) where the constant of proportionality R is called the resistance of the conductor.

tex.back:
or, $V = RI$
where the constant of proportionality $R$ is called the resistance of the conductor.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Ohm's law.
cards.back: Ohm's law: The electric current I flowing through a substance is proportional to the voltage V across its ends
cards.quote: Ohm's law: The electric current I flowing through a substance is proportional to the voltage V across its ends

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of resistance?
cards.back: The SI units of resistance is ohm
cards.quote: The SI units of resistance is ohm

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is the ohm, the unit of resistance, expressed in volt and ampere?
cards.back: The unit of resistance is ohm: 1W = 1 V A–1.
cards.quote: The unit of resistance is ohm: 1W = 1 V A–1.

tex.back: The unit of resistance is ohm: $1\ \Omega = 1\ \text{V A}^{-1}$.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The resistance R not only depends on the material of the conductor but also on the ____ of the conductor.
cards.back: The resistance R not only depends on the material of the conductor but also on the dimensions of the conductor.
cards.quote: The resistance R not only depends on the material of the conductor but also on the dimensions of the conductor.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens to the resistance of a conductor when its length is doubled?
cards.back: doubling the length of a conductor doubles the resistance.
cards.quote: Thus, doubling the length of a conductor doubles the resistance.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens to the resistance of a conductor when the area of its cross-section is halved?
cards.back: halving the area of the cross-section of a conductor doubles the resistance.
cards.quote: Thus, halving the area of the cross-section of a conductor doubles the resistance.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the resistance of a conductor depend on its length?
cards.back: In general, then resistance is proportional to length
cards.quote: In general, then resistance is proportional to length

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the resistance of a conductor depend on its cross-sectional area?
cards.back: In general, then the resistance R is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area
cards.quote: In general, then the resistance R is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: resistance R of a conductor of length l, cross-sectional area A and resistivity ρ
cards.back:
R=ρ l A
where the constant of proportionality r depends on the material of the conductor but not on its dimensions. r is called resistivity.
cards.quote: R=ρ l A (3.9) where the constant of proportionality r depends on the material of the conductor but not on its dimensions. r is called resistivity.

tex.back:
$$R = \rho\frac{l}{A}$$
where the constant of proportionality $\rho$ depends on the material of the conductor but not on its dimensions. $\rho$ is called resistivity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The resistance R of a conductor depends on its length and cross-sectional area through a constant of the material. What is it called?
cards.back: Resistivity is a property of the material and depends on temperature and pressure.
cards.quote: resistivity is a property of the material and depends on temperature and pressure.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define current density.
cards.back: Current per unit area (taken normal to the current), I/A, is called current density and is denoted by j.
cards.quote: Current per unit area (taken normal to the current), I/A, is called current density and is denoted by j.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of current density?
cards.back: The SI units of the current density are A/m2.
cards.quote: The SI units of the current density are A/m2.

tex.back: The SI units of the current density are $\text{A/m}^2$.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does current density j give?
cards.back: Current density j gives the amount of charge flowing per second per unit area normal to the flow
cards.quote: Current density j gives the amount of charge flowing per second per unit area normal to the flow

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: Ohm's law in vector form with current density j, field E, resistivity ρ and conductivity σ
cards.back:
E = jr
or, j = s E
cards.quote: Thus, the last equation can be written as, E = jr (3.12) or, j = s E (3.13)

tex.back:
$$\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{j}\rho$$
or, $\mathbf{j} = \sigma\mathbf{E}$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If we consider all the electrons, their average velocity will be ____ since their directions are random.
cards.back: If we consider all the electrons, their average velocity will be zero since their directions are random.
cards.quote: If we consider all the electrons, their average velocity will be zero since their directions are random.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Although electrons in a conductor are accelerated by the field, what is surprising about the average velocity they move with?
cards.back: the electrons move with an average velocity which is independent of time, although electrons are accelerated.
cards.quote: It tells us that the electrons move with an average velocity which is independent of time, although electrons are accelerated.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: drift speed v_d of electrons in terms of their acceleration a, collision time τ and the field E
cards.back:
If such collisions occur on an average at a time interval t,
vd = at = eEt/m
where a is the acceleration of the electron.
cards.quote: If such collisions occur on an average at a time interval t, vd = at = eEt/m where a is the acceleration of the electron.

tex.front: Formula: drift speed $v_d$ of electrons in terms of their acceleration $a$, collision time $\tau$ and the field $E$
tex.back:
If such collisions occur on an average at a time interval $\tau$,
$$v_d = a\tau = eE\tau/m$$
where $a$ is the acceleration of the electron.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: current density j of charge carriers of number density n, charge q and drift velocity v_d
cards.back:
j = nq vd
where n is the number density (number per unit volume) of charge carriers each of charge q, and vd is the drift velocity of the charge carriers.
cards.quote: j = nq vd where n is the number density (number per unit volume) of charge carriers each of charge q, and vd is the drift velocity of the charge carriers.

tex.front: Formula: current density $\mathbf{j}$ of charge carriers of number density $n$, charge $q$ and drift velocity $\mathbf{v}_d$
tex.back:
$$\mathbf{j} = nq\,\mathbf{v}_d$$
where $n$ is the number density (number per unit volume) of charge carriers each of charge $q$, and $\mathbf{v}_d$ is the drift velocity of the charge carriers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnitude of the current I through an area A normal to j, in terms of n, e and v_d
cards.back:
If j is normal to a cross-sectional area A and is constant over the area, the magnitude of the current I through the area is
nevd A.
cards.quote: If j is normal to a cross-sectional area A and is constant over the area, the magnitude of the current I through the area is nevd A.

tex.front: Formula: magnitude of the current $I$ through an area $A$ normal to $\mathbf{j}$, in terms of $n$, $e$ and $v_d$
tex.back:
If $\mathbf{j}$ is normal to a cross-sectional area $\mathbf{A}$ and is constant over the area, the magnitude of the current $I$ through the area is
$$nev_d A$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: conductivity σ of a metal in terms of the electron number density n, charge e, collision time τ and mass m
cards.back: σ = ne 2 τ m
cards.quote: σ = ne 2 τ m (3.23) We thus see that a very simple picture of electrical conduction reproduces Ohm’s law.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

tex.back: $$\sigma = \frac{ne^2}{m}\tau$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the direction of drift velocity of electrons relative to the electric field?
cards.back: The direction of drift velocity of conduction electrons is opposite to the electric field direction, i.e., electrons drift in the direction of increasing potential.
cards.quote: The direction of drift velocity of conduction electrons is opposite to the electric field direction, i.e., electrons drift in the direction of increasing potential.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electric field is established throughout the circuit, ____ (with the speed of light) causing at every point a local electron drift.
cards.back: Electric field is established throughout the circuit, almost instantly (with the speed of light) causing at every point a local electron drift.
cards.quote: Electric field is established throughout the circuit, almost instantly (with the speed of light) causing at every point a local electron drift.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When electrons drift in a metal from lower to higher potential, are all the free electrons moving in the same direction?
cards.back: By no means. The drift velocity is superposed over the large random velocities of electrons.
cards.quote: By no means. The drift velocity is superposed over the large random velocities of electrons.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the absence of electric field, the paths are ____; in the presence of electric field, the paths are, in general, ____.
cards.back: In the absence of electric field, the paths are straight lines; in the presence of electric field, the paths are, in general, curved.
cards.quote: In the absence of electric field, the paths are straight lines; in the presence of electric field, the paths are, in general, curved.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mobility is defined as what?
cards.back: the magnitude of the drift velocity per unit electric field
cards.quote: the magnitude of the drift velocity per unit electric field

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Is mobility positive or negative?
cards.back: Mobility is positive.
cards.quote: Mobility is positive.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of mobility?
cards.back: The SI unit of mobility is m2/Vs and is 104 of the mobility in practical units (cm2/Vs).
cards.quote: The SI unit of mobility is m2/Vs and is 104 of the mobility in practical units (cm2/Vs).

tex.back: The SI unit of mobility is $\text{m}^2/\text{Vs}$ and is $10^4$ of the mobility in practical units ($\text{cm}^2/\text{Vs}$).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mobile charge carriers in a metal, an ionised gas and an electrolyte.
cards.back:
In metals, these mobile charge carriers are electrons
in an ionised gas, they are electrons and positive charged ions
in an electrolyte, these can be both positive and negative ions
cards.quote: In metals, these mobile charge carriers are electrons; in an ionised gas, they are electrons and positive charged ions; in an electrolyte, these can be both positive and negative ions.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: mobility μ in terms of the electron charge e, the average collision time τ and the mass m
cards.back:
µ = vd = eτ Em
where t is the average collision time for electrons.
cards.quote: Hence, µ = vd = eτ Em where t is the average collision time for electrons.

tex.back:
$$\mu = \frac{v_d}{E} = \frac{e\tau}{m}$$
where $\tau$ is the average collision time for electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Ohm's law is valid for a large class of materials; what does not hold for some materials and devices in circuits?
cards.back: Although Ohm's law has been found valid over a large class of materials, there do exist materials and devices used in electric circuits where the proportionality of V and I does not hold
cards.quote: Although Ohm's law has been found valid over a large class of materials, there do exist materials and devices used in electric circuits where the proportionality of V and I does not hold

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Three ways in which Ohm's law fails.
cards.back:
(a) V depends on I non-linearly.
(b) the relation between V and I depends on the sign of V for the same absolute value of V.
(c) The relation between V and I is non-unique.
cards.quote: It fails if (a) V depends on I non-linearly. (b) the relation between V and I depends on the sign of V for the same absolute value of V. (c) The relation between V and I is non-unique.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Ohm's law is obeyed by many substances, but it is ____ of nature.
cards.back: Ohm's law is obeyed by many substances, but it is not a fundamental law of nature.
cards.quote: Ohm's law is obeyed by many substances, but it is not a fundamental law of nature.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which device shows a V-I relation that depends on the sign of V?
cards.back: This happens, for example, in a diode which we will study in Chapter 14.
cards.quote: This happens, for example, in a diode which we will study in Chapter 14.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which material shows a V-I relation with more than one V for the same current I?
cards.back: A material exhibiting such behaviour is GaAs.
cards.quote: A material exhibiting such behaviour is GaAs.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The Ohm's law asserts that the plot of I versus V is ____ i.e., R is independent of V.
cards.back: The Ohm's law asserts that the plot of I versus V is linear i.e., R is independent of V.
cards.quote: The Ohm's law asserts that the plot of I versus V is linear i.e., R is independent of V.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: V = IR defines resistance. To which devices may it be applied?
cards.back: This equation defines resistance and it may be applied to all conducting devices whether they obey Ohm's law or not.
cards.quote: This equation defines resistance and it may be applied to all conducting devices whether they obey Ohm's law or not.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which of a resistor and a diode obeys Ohm's law?
cards.back: A resistor obeys Ohm's law while a diode does not.
cards.quote: A resistor obeys Ohm's law while a diode does not.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Using E = ρj, when does a conducting material obey Ohm’s law, in terms of its resistivity ρ?
cards.back: Equation E = ρ j leads to another statement of Ohm’s law, i.e., a conducting material obeys Ohm’s law when the resistivity of the material does not depend on the magnitude and direction of applied electric field.
cards.quote: Equation E = ρ j leads to another statement of Ohm’s law, i.e., a conducting material obeys Ohm’s law when the resistivity of the material does not depend on the magnitude and direction of applied electric field.

tex.back: Equation $\mathbf{E} = \rho\,\mathbf{j}$ leads to another statement of Ohm’s law, i.e., a conducting material obeys Ohm’s law when the resistivity of the material does not depend on the magnitude and direction of applied electric field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If the field becomes ____, there are departures from Ohm's law in all cases.
cards.back: If the field becomes too strong, there are departures from Ohm's law in all cases.
cards.quote: If the field becomes too strong, there are departures from Ohm's law in all cases.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Current is a ____ although we represent current with an arrow.
cards.back: Current is a scalar although we represent current with an arrow.
cards.quote: Current is a scalar although we represent current with an arrow.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: current I through an area in terms of the current density j and the area vector ΔS
cards.back:
The current I through an area of cross-section is given by the scalar product of two vectors:
I = j . DS
where j and DS are vectors.
cards.quote: The current I through an area of cross-section is given by the scalar product of two vectors: I = j . DS where j and DS are vectors.

tex.back:
The current $I$ through an area of cross-section is given by the scalar product of two vectors:
$$I = \mathbf{j} \cdot \Delta\mathbf{S}$$
where $\mathbf{j}$ and $\Delta\mathbf{S}$ are vectors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Currents do not obey the law of ____.
cards.back: Currents do not obey the law of vector addition.
cards.quote: Currents do not obey the law of vector addition.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Classification of materials by resistivity, in increasing order.
cards.back:
conductors
semiconductors
insulators
cards.quote: The materials are classified as conductors, semiconductors and insulators depending on their resistivities, in an increasing order of their values.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In between the two are the semiconductors. These, however, have resistivities characteristically ____ with a rise in temperature.
cards.back: In between the two are the semiconductors. These, however, have resistivities characteristically decreasing with a rise in temperature.
cards.quote: In between the two are the semiconductors. These, however, have resistivities characteristically decreasing with a rise in temperature.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The resistivities of semiconductors can be decreased by adding small amount of suitable ____.
cards.back: The resistivities of semiconductors can be decreased by adding small amount of suitable impurities.
cards.quote: The resistivities of semiconductors can be decreased by adding small amount of suitable impurities.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where do semiconductors like Si and Ge lie on the resistivity scale?
cards.back: Semiconductors like Si and Ge lie roughly in the middle range of resistivity on a logarithmic scale.
cards.quote: Semiconductors like Si and Ge lie roughly in the middle range of resistivity on a logarithmic scale.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the carriers of current in most substances, and in ionic crystals and electrolytic liquids?
cards.back: In most substances, the carriers of current are electrons; in some cases, for example, ionic crystals and electrolytic liquids, positive and negative ions carry the electric current.
cards.quote: In most substances, the carriers of current are electrons; in some cases, for example, ionic crystals and electrolytic liquids, positive and negative ions carry the electric current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The temperature coefficient of resistivity is defined as what?
cards.back: the fractional increase in resistivity per unit increase in temperature
cards.quote: the fractional increase in resistivity per unit increase in temperature

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: resistivity of a metallic conductor at temperature T in terms of its value at a reference temperature T₀
cards.back:
Over a limited range of temperatures, that is not too large, the resistivity of a metallic conductor is approximately given by,
rT = r0 [1 + a (T–T0)]
where rT is the resistivity at a temperature T and r0 is the same at a reference temperature T0.
cards.quote: Over a limited range of temperatures, that is not too large, the resistivity of a metallic conductor is approximately given by, rT = r0 [1 + a (T–T0)] (3.26) where rT is the resistivity at a temperature T and r0 is the same at a reference temperature T0.

tex.back:
Over a limited range of temperatures, that is not too large, the resistivity of a metallic conductor is approximately given by,
$$\rho_T = \rho_0\,[1 + \alpha\,(T - T_0)]$$
where $\rho_T$ is the resistivity at a temperature $T$ and $\rho_0$ is the same at a reference temperature $T_0$.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the dimension of the temperature co-efficient of resistivity α, and is α positive or negative for metals?
cards.back: a is called the temperature co-efficient of resistivity, and from Eq. (3.26), the dimension of a is (Temperature)–1. For metals, a is positive.
cards.quote: a is called the temperature co-efficient of resistivity, and from Eq. (3.26), the dimension of a is (Temperature)–1. For metals, a is positive.

tex.back: $\alpha$ is called the temperature co-efficient of resistivity, and from Eq. (3.26), the dimension of $\alpha$ is $(\text{Temperature})^{-1}$. For metals, $\alpha$ is positive.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which alloy of nickel, iron and chromium shows a very weak dependence of resistivity on temperature?
cards.back: Some materials like Nichrome (which is an alloy of nickel, iron and chromium) exhibit a very weak dependence of resistivity with temperature.
cards.quote: Some materials like Nichrome (which is an alloy of nickel, iron and chromium) exhibit a very weak dependence of resistivity with temperature.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Unlike metals, the resistivities of semiconductors ____ with increasing temperatures.
cards.back: Unlike metals, the resistivities of semiconductors decrease with increasing temperatures.
cards.quote: Unlike metals, the resistivities of semiconductors decrease with increasing temperatures.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: resistivity ρ of a metal in terms of the electron number density n, charge e, collision time τ and mass m
cards.back:
From this equation, resistivity of a material is given by
ρ = 1 σ = m n e 2τ
cards.quote: From this equation, resistivity of a material is given by ρ = 1 σ = m n e 2τ (3.27)

tex.back:
From this equation, resistivity of a material is given by
$$\rho = \frac{1}{\sigma} = \frac{m}{ne^2\tau}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: As we increase temperature, average speed of the electrons, which act as the carriers of current, increases resulting in ____.
cards.back: As we increase temperature, average speed of the electrons, which act as the carriers of current, increases resulting in more frequent collisions.
cards.quote: As we increase temperature, average speed of the electrons, which act as the carriers of current, increases resulting in more frequent collisions.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: During collisions, the energy gained by the charges thus is shared with the atoms. The atoms vibrate more vigorously, i.e., the conductor ____.
cards.back: During collisions, the energy gained by the charges thus is shared with the atoms. The atoms vibrate more vigorously, i.e., the conductor heats up.
cards.quote: During collisions, the energy gained by the charges thus is shared with the atoms. The atoms vibrate more vigorously, i.e., the conductor heats up.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define power dissipated in a conductor.
cards.back: The energy dissipated per unit time is the power dissipated
cards.quote: The energy dissipated per unit time is the power dissipated

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: power dissipated in terms of potential difference V and current I.
cards.back: P=IV
cards.quote: P=IV

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: power dissipated in a resistor R in terms of the current I through it and the voltage V across it
cards.back:
Using Ohm’s law V = IR, we get
P = I 2 R = V 2/R
cards.quote: Using Ohm’s law V = IR, we get P = I 2 R = V 2/R (3.33)

tex.back:
Using Ohm’s law $V = IR$, we get
$$P = I^2 R = V^2/R$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the power loss in a conductor of resistance R carrying a current I called?
cards.back: "ohmic loss"
cards.quote: as the power loss ("ohmic loss") in a conductor of resistance R carrying a current I.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a simple circuit with a cell, what supplies the power dissipated in the conductor?
cards.back: In the simple circuit shown with a cell (Fig.3.11), it is the chemical energy of the cell which supplies this power for as long as it can.
cards.quote: In the simple circuit shown with a cell (Fig.3.11), it is the chemical energy of the cell which supplies this power for as long as it can.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Using electricity at such voltages is not safe and hence at the other end, a device called a ____ lowers the voltage to a value suitable for use.
cards.back: Using electricity at such voltages is not safe and hence at the other end, a device called a transformer lowers the voltage to a value suitable for use.
cards.quote: Using electricity at such voltages is not safe and hence at the other end, a device called a transformer lowers the voltage to a value suitable for use.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Basically a cell has two ____, called the positive (P) and the negative (N)
cards.back: Basically a cell has two electrodes, called the positive (P) and the negative (N)
cards.quote: Basically a cell has two electrodes, called the positive (P) and the negative (N)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the electromotive force (emf) of a source.
cards.back: The work done per unit charge by the source in taking the charge from lower to higher potential energy (i.e., from one terminal of the source to the other) is called the electromotive force, or emf, of the source.
cards.quote: The work done per unit charge by the source in taking the charge from lower to higher potential energy (i.e., from one terminal of the source to the other) is called the electromotive force, or emf, of the source.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Note that the emf is ____; it is the voltage difference between the two terminals of a source in open circuit.
cards.back: Note that the emf is not a force; it is the voltage difference between the two terminals of a source in open circuit.
cards.quote: Note that the emf is not a force; it is the voltage difference between the two terminals of a source in open circuit.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: To maintain a steady current, we must have a ____ in which an external agency moves electric charge from lower to higher potential energy.
cards.back: To maintain a steady current, we must have a closed circuit in which an external agency moves electric charge from lower to higher potential energy.
cards.quote: To maintain a steady current, we must have a closed circuit in which an external agency moves electric charge from lower to higher potential energy.

cards.subject: physics

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Kirchhoff's junction rule.

cards.quote: Junction rule: At any junction, the sum of the currents entering the junction is equal to the sum of currents leaving the junction

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Kirchhoff's loop rule.
cards.back: Loop rule: The algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop involving resistors and cells in the loop is zero
cards.quote: Loop rule: The algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop involving resistors and cells in the loop is zero

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The proof of this rule follows from the fact that when currents are steady, there is ____ at any junction or at any point in a line.
cards.back: The proof of this rule follows from the fact that when currents are steady, there is no accumulation of charges at any junction or at any point in a line.
cards.quote: The proof of this rule follows from the fact that when currents are steady, there is no accumulation of charges at any junction or at any point in a line.

cards.subject: physics

cards.quote: Thus starting with any point if we come back to the same point, the total change must be zero.

cards.front: Define the work function of a metal.
cards.back: A certain minimum amount of energy is required to be given to an electron to pull it out from the surface of the metal. This minimum energy required by an electron to escape from the metal surface is called the work function of the metal.
cards.quote: A certain minimum amount of energy is required to be given to an electron to pull it out from the surface of the metal. This minimum energy required by an electron to escape from the metal surface is called the work function of the metal.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Which symbol denotes the work function of a metal, and in what unit is it measured?
cards.back: It is generally denoted by f0 and measured in eV (electron volt).

cards.subject: physics

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Name the three physical processes that supply the energy for electron emission from a metal.
cards.back:
Thermionic emission
Field emission
Photoelectric emission
cards.quote: (i) Thermionic emission: By suitably heating, sufficient thermal energy can be imparted to the free electrons to enable them to come out of the metal. (ii) Field emission: By applying a very strong electric field (of the order of 108 V m–1) to a metal, electrons can be pulled out of the metal, as in a spark plug. (iii) Photoelectric emission: When light of suitable frequency illuminates a metal surface, electrons are emitted from the metal surface. These photo(light)-generated electrons are called photoelectrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: ____: By suitably heating, sufficient thermal energy can be imparted to the free electrons to enable them to come out of the metal.

cards.quote: Thermionic emission: By suitably heating, sufficient thermal energy can be imparted to the free electrons to enable them to come out of the metal.

cards.quote: Photoelectric emission : When light of suitable frequency illuminates a metal surface, electrons are emitted from the metal surface.

cards.subject: physics

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Who discovered photoelectric emission, and in which year?
cards.back: The phenomenon of photoelectric emission was discovered in 1887 by Heinrich Hertz (1857-1894), during his electromagnetic wave experiments.
cards.quote: The phenomenon of photoelectric emission was discovered in 1887 by Heinrich Hertz (1857-1894), during his electromagnetic wave experiments.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Near a metal surface, electrons that absorb enough energy from incident light overcome what attraction?
cards.back: When light falls on a metal surface, some electrons near the surface absorb enough energy from the incident radiation to overcome the attraction of the positive ions in the material of the surface.
cards.quote: When light falls on a metal surface, some electrons near the surface absorb enough energy from the incident radiation to overcome the attraction of the positive ions in the material of the surface.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Which two scientists investigated photoelectric emission in detail during 1886-1902?
cards.back: Wilhelm Hallwachs and Philipp Lenard investigated the phenomenon of photoelectric emission in detail during 1886-1902.
cards.quote: Wilhelm Hallwachs and Philipp Lenard investigated the phenomenon of photoelectric emission in detail during 1886-1902.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What is the threshold frequency (Hallwachs and Lenard's observation)?
cards.back: Hallwachs and Lenard also observed that when ultraviolet light fell on the emitter plate, no electrons were emitted at all when the frequency of the incident light was smaller than a certain minimum value, called the threshold frequency.
cards.quote: Hallwachs and Lenard also observed that when ultraviolet light fell on the emitter plate, no electrons were emitted at all when the frequency of the incident light was smaller than a certain minimum value, called the threshold frequency.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: On what does the threshold frequency depend?
cards.back: Hallwachs and Lenard also observed that when ultraviolet light fell on the emitter plate, no electrons were emitted at all when the frequency of the incident light was smaller than a certain minimum value, called the threshold frequency. This minimum frequency depends on the nature of the material of the emitter plate.
cards.quote: Hallwachs and Lenard also observed that when ultraviolet light fell on the emitter plate, no electrons were emitted at all when the frequency of the incident light was smaller than a certain minimum value, called the threshold frequency. This minimum frequency depends on the nature of the material of the emitter plate.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Which metals respond only to ultraviolet light (short wavelength) for photoelectric emission?
cards.back: It was found that certain metals like zinc, cadmium, magnesium, etc., responded only to ultraviolet light, having short wavelength, to cause electron emission from the surface.
cards.quote: It was found that certain metals like zinc, cadmium, magnesium, etc., responded only to ultraviolet light, having short wavelength, to cause electron emission from the surface.

cards.subject: physics

cards.front: Which alkali metals are sensitive even to visible light in photoelectric emission?
cards.back: However, some alkali metals such as lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium and rubidium were sensitive even to visible light.
cards.quote: However, some alkali metals such as lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium and rubidium were sensitive even to visible light.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What is the photoelectric effect?
cards.back: Photoelectric effect is the phenomenon of emission of electrons by metals when illuminated by light of suitable frequency.
cards.quote: Photoelectric effect is the phenomenon of emission of electrons by metals when illuminated by light of suitable frequency.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Photoelectric effect involves conversion of ____ into ____.
cards.back: Photoelectric effect involves conversion of light energy into electrical energy.
cards.quote: Photoelectric effect involves conversion of light energy into electrical energy.

cards.front: Name the four factors with which photocurrent variation is studied in the experimental arrangement.
cards.back:
intensity of radiation
frequency of incident radiation
the potential difference between the plates A and C
the nature of the material of plate C
cards.quote: We can use the experimental arrangement of Fig. 11.1 to study the variation of photocurrent with (a) intensity of radiation, (b) frequency of incident radiation, (c) the potential difference between the plates A and C, and (d) the nature of the material of plate C.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: With frequency and potential fixed, how does photocurrent vary with the intensity of incident light?
cards.back: Keeping the frequency of the incident radiation and the potential fixed, the intensity of light is varied and the resulting photoelectric current is measured each time. It is found that the photocurrent increases linearly with intensity of incident light
cards.quote: Keeping the frequency of the incident radiation and the potential fixed, the intensity of light is varied and the resulting photoelectric current is measured each time. It is found that the photocurrent increases linearly with intensity of incident light

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: How is the number of photoelectrons emitted per second related to the intensity of incident radiation?
cards.back: The photocurrent is directly proportional to the number of photoelectrons emitted per second. This implies that the number of photoelectrons emitted per second is directly proportional to the intensity of incident radiation.
cards.quote: The photocurrent is directly proportional to the number of photoelectrons emitted per second. This implies that the number of photoelectrons emitted per second is directly proportional to the intensity of incident radiation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What is saturation current in the photoelectric effect?
cards.back: This maximum value of the photoelectric current is called saturation current. Saturation current corresponds to the case when all the photoelectrons emitted by the emitter plate C reach the collector plate A.
cards.quote: This maximum value of the photoelectric current is called saturation current. Saturation current corresponds to the case when all the photoelectrons emitted by the emitter plate C reach the collector plate A.

cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Define the cut-off (stopping) potential.
cards.back: For a particular frequency of incident radiation, the minimum negative (retarding) potential V0 given to the plate A for which the photocurrent stops or becomes zero is called the cut-off or stopping potential.
cards.quote: For a particular frequency of incident radiation, the minimum negative (retarding) potential V0 given to the plate A for which the photocurrent stops or becomes zero is called the cut-off or stopping potential.

cards.back: All the photoelectrons emitted from the metal do not have the same energy.
cards.quote: All the photoelectrons emitted from the metal do not have the same energy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Formula: maximum kinetic energy Kmax of photoelectrons in terms of the stopping potential V₀
cards.back:
Photoelectric current is zero when the stopping potential is sufficient to repel even the most energetic photoelectrons, with the maximum kinetic energy (Kmax), so that
Kmax = e V0
cards.quote: Photoelectric current is zero when the stopping potential is sufficient to repel even the most energetic photoelectrons, with the maximum kinetic energy (Kmax), so that Kmax = e V0

cards.back: For a given frequency of the incident radiation, the stopping potential is independent of its intensity.

cards.back: The stopping potential is more negative for higher frequencies of incident radiation.
cards.quote: The stopping potential is more negative for higher frequencies of incident radiation.

cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation

cards.subject: physics

cards.quote: greater the frequency of incident light, greater is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

cards.front: Define threshold frequency.
cards.back: For a given photosensitive material, there exists a certain minimum cut-off frequency of the incident radiation, called the threshold frequency, below which no emission of photoelectrons takes place, no matter how intense the incident light is.
cards.quote: For a given photosensitive material, there exists a certain minimum cut-off frequency of the incident radiation, called the threshold frequency, below which no emission of photoelectrons takes place, no matter how intense the incident light is.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: If the frequency exceeds the threshold frequency, how soon does photoelectric emission start?
cards.back: If frequency of the incident radiation exceeds the threshold frequency, the photoelectric emission starts instantaneously without any apparent time lag, even if the incident radiation is very dim.
cards.quote: if frequency of the incident radiation exceeds the threshold frequency, the photoelectric emission starts instantaneously without any apparent time lag, even if the incident radiation is very dim.

cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Who proposed a radically new picture of electromagnetic radiation in 1905 to explain the photoelectric effect?
cards.back: In 1905, Albert Einstein (1879 -1955) proposed a radically new picture of electromagnetic radiation to explain photoelectric effect.
cards.quote: In 1905, Albert Einstein (1879 -1955) proposed a radically new picture of electromagnetic radiation to explain photoelectric effect.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Radiation energy is built up of discrete units - the so called ____ of energy of radiation.
cards.back: Radiation energy is built up of discrete units - the so called quanta of energy of radiation.
cards.quote: Radiation energy is built up of discrete units - the so called quanta of energy of radiation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Formula: Einstein’s photoelectric equation for the maximum kinetic energy Kmax
cards.back:
In photoelectric effect, an electron absorbs a quantum of energy (hn ) of radiation. If this quantum of energy absorbed exceeds the minimum energy needed for the electron to escape from the metal surface (work function f0), the electron is emitted with maximum kinetic energy
Kmax = hn – f0
cards.quote: In photoelectric effect, an electron absorbs a quantum of energy (hn ) of radiation. If this quantum of energy absorbed exceeds the minimum energy needed for the electron to escape from the metal surface (work function f0), the electron is emitted with maximum kinetic energy Kmax = hn – f0

tex.back:
In photoelectric effect, an electron absorbs a quantum of energy ($h\nu$) of radiation. If this quantum of energy absorbed exceeds the minimum energy needed for the electron to escape from the metal surface (work function $\phi_0$), the electron is emitted with maximum kinetic energy
$$K_{\text{max}} = h\nu - \phi_0$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Note that the intensity of light of a given frequency is determined by the ____ incident per second.
cards.back: Note that the intensity of light of a given frequency is determined by the number of photons incident per second.
cards.quote: Note that the intensity of light of a given frequency is determined by the number of photons incident per second.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: In Einstein's picture, increasing intensity increases what, while maximum kinetic energy depends on each photon's energy?
cards.back: Increasing the intensity will increase the number of emitted electrons per second. However, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is determined by the energy of each photon.
cards.quote: Increasing the intensity will increase the number of emitted electrons per second. However, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is determined by the energy of each photon.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: In Einstein's picture, photoelectric effect arises from the absorption of what by what?
cards.back: In Einstein's picture, photoelectric effect arises from the absorption of a single quantum of radiation by a single electron.
cards.quote: in Einstein's picture, photoelectric effect arises from the absorption of a single quantum of radiation by a single electron.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Low intensity does not mean ____ in emission, since the basic elementary process is the same.
cards.back: Low intensity does not mean delay in emission, since the basic elementary process is the same.
cards.quote: Low intensity does not mean delay in emission, since the basic elementary process is the same.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: From Einstein’s equation, what is the slope of the straight line of V₀ versus ν?
cards.back: It predicts that the V0 versus n curve is a straight line with slope = (h/e)
cards.quote: It predicts that the V0 versus n curve is a straight line with slope = (h/e),

tex.back: It predicts that the $V_0$ versus $\nu$ curve is a straight line with slope $= (h/e)$

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Einstein's photoelectric equation is in accordance with the ____ as applied to the photon absorption by an electron in the metal.
cards.back: Einstein's photoelectric equation is in accordance with the energy conservation law as applied to the photon absorption by an electron in the metal.
cards.quote: Einstein's photoelectric equation is in accordance with the energy conservation law as applied to the photon absorption by an electron in the metal.
cards.note: The equation: maximum kinetic energy = photon energy (Planck's constant times frequency) minus the work function.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: The stopping potential is directly related to the ____ of electrons emitted
cards.back: The stopping potential is directly related to the maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted
cards.quote: The stopping potential is directly related to the maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted
cards.note: Stopping potential times the electron charge equals the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Which scientist performed experiments in 1906-1916 aimed at disproving Einstein's photoelectric equation?
cards.back: During 1906-1916, Millikan performed a series of experiments on photoelectric effect, aimed at disproving Einstein's photoelectric equation.
cards.quote: During 1906-1916, Millikan performed a series of experiments on photoelectric effect, aimed at disproving Einstein's photoelectric equation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What did Millikan determine from the slope of the stopping potential versus frequency line for sodium?
cards.back: He measured the slope of the straight line obtained for sodium, similar to that shown in Fig. 11.5. Using the known value of e, he determined the value of Planck's constant h.
cards.quote: He measured the slope of the straight line obtained for sodium, similar to that shown in Fig. 11.5. Using the known value of e, he determined the value of Planck's constant h.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What value of Planck’s constant h does NCERT quote when it describes Millikan’s result?
cards.back: (= 6.626 × 10–34J s) determined in an entirely different context.
cards.quote: This value was close to the value of Planck’s contant (= 6.626 × 10–34J s) determined in an entirely different context.

tex.back: $(= 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s})$ determined in an entirely different context.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Who proved the validity of Einstein's photoelectric equation in 1916?
cards.back: In this way, in 1916, Millikan proved the validity of Einstein's photoelectric equation, instead of disproving it.
cards.quote: In this way, in 1916, Millikan proved the validity of Einstein's photoelectric equation, instead of disproving it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What name was later given to the particle associated with the light quantum?
cards.back: A definite value of energy as well as momentum is a strong sign that the light quantum can be associated with a particle. This particle was later named photon.
cards.quote: A definite value of energy as well as momentum is a strong sign that the light quantum can be associated with a particle. This particle was later named photon.

source.section: Particle nature of light: the photon

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Whose 1924 experiment on scattering of X-rays from electrons further confirmed the particle-like behaviour of light?
cards.back: The particle-like behaviour of light was further confirmed, in 1924, by the experiment of A.H. Compton (1892-1962) on scattering of X-rays from electrons.
cards.quote: The particle-like behaviour of light was further confirmed, in 1924, by the experiment of A.H. Compton (1892-1962) on scattering of X-rays from electrons.

source.section: Particle nature of light: the photon

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: In interaction of radiation with matter, radiation behaves as if it is made up of ____ called photons.
cards.back: In interaction of radiation with matter, radiation behaves as if it is made up of particles called photons.
cards.quote: In interaction of radiation with matter, radiation behaves as if it is made up of particles called photons.

source.section: Particle nature of light: the photon

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Formula: energy E and momentum p of a photon of frequency ν and wavelength λ
cards.back:
Each photon has energy E (=hν) and momentum p (= h ν/c), and speed c, the speed of light.
All photons of light of a particular frequency ν, or wavelength λ, have the same energy E (=hν = hc/λ) and momentum p (= hν/c= h/λ)
cards.quote: Each photon has energy E (=hν) and momentum p (= h ν/c), and speed c, the speed of light. (iii) All photons of light of a particular frequency ν, or wavelength λ, have the same energy E (=hν = hc/λ) and momentum p (= hν/c= h/λ),

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: How does the energy of a photon depend on the intensity of radiation?
cards.back: By increasing the intensity of light of given wavelength, there is only an increase in the number of photons per second crossing a given area, with each photon having the same energy. Thus, photon energy is independent of intensity of radiation.
cards.quote: By increasing the intensity of light of given wavelength, there is only an increase in the number of photons per second crossing a given area, with each photon having the same energy. Thus, photon energy is independent of intensity of radiation.

source.section: Particle nature of light: the photon

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Photons are ____ and are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
cards.back: Photons are electrically neutral and are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
cards.quote: Photons are electrically neutral and are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

source.section: Particle nature of light: the photon

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: In a photon-particle collision, total energy and momentum are conserved; which quantity may not be?
cards.back: In a photon-particle collision (such as photon-electron collision), the total energy and total momentum are conserved. However, the number of photons may not be conserved in a collision.
cards.quote: In a photon-particle collision (such as photon-electron collision), the total energy and total momentum are conserved. However, the number of photons may not be conserved in a collision.

source.section: Particle nature of light: the photon

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Name the phenomena in which the wave nature of light shows up.
cards.back:
interference
diffraction
polarisation
cards.quote: The wave nature of light shows up in the phenomena of interference, diffraction and polarisation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: In which two effects, involving energy and momentum transfer, does radiation behave as a bunch of photons?
cards.back: The wave nature of light shows up in the phenomena of interference, diffraction and polarisation. On the other hand, in photoelectric effect and Compton effect which involve energy and momentum transfer, radiation behaves as if it is made up of a bunch of particles – the photons.
cards.quote: The wave nature of light shows up in the phenomena of interference, diffraction and polarisation. On the other hand, in photoelectric effect and Compton effect which involve energy and momentum transfer, radiation behaves as if it is made up of a bunch of particles – the photons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Whether a particle or wave description is best suited for understanding an experiment depends on the ____.
cards.back: Whether a particle or wave description is best suited for understanding an experiment depends on the nature of the experiment.
cards.quote: Whether a particle or wave description is best suited for understanding an experiment depends on the nature of the experiment.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Who put forward the hypothesis in 1924 that moving particles of matter display wave-like properties?
cards.back: In 1924, the French physicist Louis Victor de Broglie (pronounced as de Broy) (1892-1987) put forward the bold hypothesis that moving particles of matter should display wave-like properties under suitable conditions.
cards.quote: In 1924, the French physicist Louis Victor de Broglie (pronounced as de Broy) (1892-1987) put forward the bold hypothesis that moving particles of matter should display wave-like properties under suitable conditions.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: He reasoned that nature was symmetrical and that the two basic physical entities - ____, must have symmetrical character.
cards.back: He reasoned that nature was symmetrical and that the two basic physical entities - matter and energy, must have symmetrical character.
cards.quote: He reasoned that nature was symmetrical and that the two basic physical entities - matter and energy, must have symmetrical character.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Formula: de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m and speed v
cards.back:
De Broglie proposed that the wave length l associated with a particle of momentum p is given as
l = h h p m v =
where m is the mass of the particle and v its speed.
Equation (11.5) is known as the de Broglie relation and the wavelength l of the matter wave is called de Broglie wavelength.
cards.quote: De Broglie proposed that the wave length l associated with a particle of momentum p is given as l = h h p m v = (11.5) where m is the mass of the particle and v its speed. Equation (11.5) is known as the de Broglie relation and the wavelength l of the matter wave is called de Broglie wavelength.

tex.back:
De Broglie proposed that the wave length $\lambda$ associated with a particle of momentum $p$ is given as
$$\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}$$
where $m$ is the mass of the particle and $v$ its speed.
Equation (11.5) is known as the de Broglie relation and the wavelength $\lambda$ of the matter wave is called de Broglie wavelength.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: From the de Broglie relation, for which particles is the wavelength λ smaller?
cards.back: Clearly, from Eq. (11.5 ), l is smaller for a heavier particle ( large m ) or more energetic particle (large v).
cards.quote: Clearly, from Eq. (11.5 ), l is smaller for a heavier particle ( large m ) or more energetic particle (large v).

tex.back: Clearly, from Eq. (11.5), $\lambda$ is smaller for a heavier particle (large $m$) or more energetic particle (large $v$).

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What are matter waves (de Broglie waves)?
cards.back: The waves associated with the moving material particles are called matter waves or de Broglie waves.
cards.quote: The waves associated with the moving material particles are called matter waves or de Broglie waves.
cards.note: De Broglie wavelength = Planck's constant divided by the momentum (mass times speed) of the particle.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: The de Broglie wavelength is independent of the ____ of the material particle.
cards.back: The de Broglie wavelength is independent of the charge and nature of the material particle.
cards.quote: The de Broglie wavelength is independent of the charge and nature of the material particle.
cards.note: The wavelength depends only on the particle's momentum (mass and speed), not on its charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Why do macroscopic objects in daily life not show wave-like properties (de Broglie wavelength of a ball)?
cards.back: This wavelength is so small that it is beyond any measurement. This is the reason why macroscopic objects in our daily life do not show wavelike properties.
cards.quote: This wavelength is so small that it is beyond any measurement. This is the reason why macroscopic objects in our daily life do not show wavelike properties.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: In which domain is the wave character of particles significant and measurable?
cards.back: In the sub-atomic domain, the wave character of particles is significant and measurable.
cards.quote: in the sub-atomic domain, the wave character of particles is significant and measurable.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What is the crucial discriminator between the wave-picture and photon-picture of photoelectric effect?
cards.back: Observations on the stopping potential (its independence of intensity and dependence on frequency) are the crucial discriminator between the wave-picture and photon-picture of photoelectric effect.
cards.quote: Observations on the stopping potential (its independence of intensity and dependence on frequency) are the crucial discriminator between the wave-picture and photon-picture of photoelectric effect.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Why is the energy needed to come out of a metal different for different electrons?
cards.back: Because of the energy distribution of free electrons in a metal, the energy required by an electron to come out of the metal is different for different electrons.
cards.quote: Because of the energy distribution of free electrons in a metal, the energy required by an electron to come out of the metal is different for different electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does electrostatics deal with?
cards.back: Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges.
cards.quote: Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does static mean?
cards.back: Static means anything that does not move or change with time.
cards.quote: Static means anything that does not move or change with time.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The name electricity is coined from the Greek word ____ meaning amber.
cards.back: The name electricity is coined from the Greek word elektron meaning amber.
cards.quote: The name electricity is coined from the Greek word elektron meaning amber.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: There are two kinds of electrification and we find that (i) ____ charges repel and (ii) ____ charges attract each other.
cards.back: There are two kinds of electrification and we find that (i) like charges repel and (ii) unlike charges attract each other.
cards.quote: There are two kinds of electrification and we find that (i) like charges repel and (ii) unlike charges attract each other.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the polarity of charge?
cards.back: The property which differentiates the two kinds of charges is called the polarity of charge.
cards.quote: The property which differentiates the two kinds of charges is called the polarity of charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who named the two kinds of charges positive and negative?
cards.back: Therefore, the charges were named as positive and negative by the American scientist Benjamin Franklin.
cards.quote: Therefore, the charges were named as positive and negative by the American scientist Benjamin Franklin.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: By convention, which bodies carry positive charge and which negative charge?
cards.back: By convention, the charge on glass rod or cat's fur is called positive and that on plastic rod or silk is termed negative.
cards.quote: By convention, the charge on glass rod or cat's fur is called positive and that on plastic rod or silk is termed negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When is an object said to be electrified, and when electrically neutral?
cards.back: If an object possesses an electric charge, it is said to be electrified or charged. When it has no charge it is said to be electrically neutral.
cards.quote: If an object possesses an electric charge, it is said to be electrified or charged. When it has no charge it is said to be electrically neutral.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A simple apparatus to detect charge on a body is the ____.
cards.back: A simple apparatus to detect charge on a body is the gold-leaf electroscope.
cards.quote: A simple apparatus to detect charge on a body is the gold-leaf electroscope.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When a charged object touches the metal knob at the top of the rod, charge flows on to the leaves and they ____.
cards.back: When a charged object touches the metal knob at the top of the rod, charge flows on to the leaves and they diverge.
cards.quote: When a charged object touches the metal knob at the top of the rod, charge flows on to the leaves and they diverge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which everyday forces are basically electrical in nature?
cards.back: Forces that hold the molecules together, forces that hold atoms together in a solid, the adhesive force of glue, forces associated with surface tension, all are basically electrical in nature, arising from the forces between charged particles.
cards.quote: Forces that hold the molecules together, forces that hold atoms together in a solid, the adhesive force of glue, forces associated with surface tension, all are basically electrical in nature, arising from the forces between charged particles.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In solids, some of the ____, being less tightly bound in the atom, are the charges which are transferred from one body to the other.
cards.back: In solids, some of the electrons, being less tightly bound in the atom, are the charges which are transferred from one body to the other.
cards.quote: In solids, some of the electrons, being less tightly bound in the atom, are the charges which are transferred from one body to the other.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does a body become positively charged and how negatively charged?
cards.back: A body can thus be charged positively by losing some of its electrons. Similarly, a body can be charged negatively by gaining electrons.
cards.quote: A body can thus be charged positively by losing some of its electrons. Similarly, a body can be charged negatively by gaining electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, what is transferred and which becomes positive?
cards.back: When we rub a glass rod with silk, some of the electrons from the rod are transferred to the silk cloth. Thus the rod gets positively charged and the silk gets negatively charged.
cards.quote: When we rub a glass rod with silk, some of the electrons from the rod are transferred to the silk cloth. Thus the rod gets positively charged and the silk gets negatively charged.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: No new charge is ____ in the process of rubbing.
cards.back: No new charge is created in the process of rubbing.
cards.quote: No new charge is created in the process of rubbing.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: To electrify a neutral body, we need to ____ or remove one kind of charge.
cards.back: To electrify a neutral body, we need to add or remove one kind of charge.
cards.quote: To electrify a neutral body, we need to add or remove one kind of charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are insulators? Name some.
cards.back: Most of the non-metals like glass, porcelain, plastic, nylon, wood offer high resistance to the passage of electricity through them. They are called insulators.
cards.quote: Most of the non-metals like glass, porcelain, plastic, nylon, wood offer high resistance to the passage of electricity through them. They are called insulators.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Conductor vs insulator: where does transferred charge go?
cards.back: When some charge is transferred to a conductor, it readily gets distributed over the entire surface of the conductor. In contrast, if some charge is put on an insulator, it stays at the same place.
cards.quote: When some charge is transferred to a conductor, it readily gets distributed over the entire surface of the conductor. In contrast, if some charge is put on an insulator, it stays at the same place.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the third category of materials besides conductors and insulators?
cards.back: There is a third category called semiconductors, which offer resistance to the movement of charges which is intermediate between the conductors and insulators.
cards.quote: There is a third category called semiconductors, which offer resistance to the movement of charges which is intermediate between the conductors and insulators.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When are charged bodies treated as point charges?
cards.back: If the sizes of charged bodies are very small as compared to the distances between them, we treat them as point charges. All the charge content of the body is assumed to be concentrated at one point in space.
cards.quote: If the sizes of charged bodies are very small as compared to the distances between them, we treat them as point charges. All the charge content of the body is assumed to be concentrated at one point in space.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Charge has magnitude but no ____, similar to mass.
cards.back: Charge has magnitude but no direction, similar to mass.
cards.quote: Charge has magnitude but no direction, similar to mass.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mass vs charge: the difference in sign.
cards.back: Mass of a body is always positive whereas a charge can be either positive or negative.
cards.quote: Mass of a body is always positive whereas a charge can be either positive or negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens to the total charge of an isolated system of charged bodies when charges get redistributed?
cards.back: Within an isolated system consisting of many charged bodies, due to interactions among the bodies, charges may get redistributed but it is found that the total charge of the isolated system is always conserved.
cards.quote: Within an isolated system consisting of many charged bodies, due to interactions among the bodies, charges may get redistributed but it is found that the total charge of the isolated system is always conserved.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Nature creates charged particles: what does a neutron turn into, and why is total charge conserved?
cards.back: Sometimes nature creates charged particles: a neutron turns into a proton and an electron. The proton and electron thus created have equal and opposite charges and the total charge is zero before and after the creation.
cards.quote: Sometimes nature creates charged particles: a neutron turns into a proton and an electron. The proton and electron thus created have equal and opposite charges and the total charge is zero before and after the creation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is quantisation of charge?
cards.back: The fact that electric charge is always an integral multiple of e is termed as quantisation of charge.
cards.quote: The fact that electric charge is always an integral multiple of e is termed as quantisation of charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Experimentally it is established that all free charges are ____ multiples of a basic unit of charge denoted by e.
cards.back: Experimentally it is established that all free charges are integral multiples of a basic unit of charge denoted by e.
cards.quote: Experimentally it is established that all free charges are integral multiples of a basic unit of charge denoted by e.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: charge on a body in terms of the basic unit of charge e.
cards.back: q = ne where n is any integer, positive or negative.
cards.quote: q = ne where n is any integer, positive or negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The basic unit of charge e is the charge carried by which particles?
cards.back: This basic unit of charge is the charge that an electron or proton carries.
cards.quote: This basic unit of charge is the charge that an electron or proton carries.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who first suggested quantisation of charge, through which experimental laws?
cards.back: The quantisation of charge was first suggested by the experimental laws of electrolysis discovered by English experimentalist Faraday.
cards.quote: The quantisation of charge was first suggested by the experimental laws of electrolysis discovered by English experimentalist Faraday.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who experimentally demonstrated quantisation of charge, and in which year?
cards.back: It was experimentally demonstrated by Millikan in 1912.
cards.quote: It was experimentally demonstrated by Millikan in 1912.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of charge and its symbol?
cards.back: In the International System (SI) of Units, a unit of charge is called a coulomb and is denoted by the symbol C.
cards.quote: In the International System (SI) of Units, a unit of charge is called a coulomb and is denoted by the symbol C.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define one coulomb in terms of current.
cards.back: In terms of this definition, one coulomb is the charge flowing through a wire in 1 s if the current is 1 A (ampere)
cards.quote: In terms of this definition, one coulomb is the charge flowing through a wire in 1 s if the current is 1 A (ampere)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: value of the basic unit of charge e in SI units.
cards.back:
In this system, the value of the basic unit of charge is
e = 1.602192 × 10–19 C
cards.quote: In this system, the value of the basic unit of charge is e = 1.602192 × 10–19 C

tex.back:
In this system, the value of the basic unit of charge is
$$e = 1.602192 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$$

cards.front: What are 1 μC (micro coulomb) and 1 mC (milli coulomb) in coulomb?
cards.back: 1 mC (micro coulomb) = 10–6 C or 1 mC (milli coulomb) = 10–3 C
cards.quote: we use smaller units 1 mC (micro coulomb) = 10–6 C or 1 mC (milli coulomb) = 10–3 C.
