cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The induced emf Blv is called ____.
cards.back: The induced emf Blv is called motional emf.
cards.quote: The induced emf Blv is called motional emf.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: motional emf across a rod of length l moving with velocity v at right angles to a uniform field B.
cards.back:
When a metal rod of length l is placed normal to a uniform magnetic field B and moved with a velocity v perpendicular to the field, the induced emf (called motional emf ) across its ends is
e = Bl v
cards.quote: When a metal rod of length l is placed normal to a uniform magnetic field B and moved with a velocity v perpendicular to the field, the induced emf (called motional emf ) across its ends is e = Bl v
cards.note: Motional emf equals the field B times the length l times the speed v, all mutually perpendicular.

tex.back:
When a metal rod of length $l$ is placed normal to a uniform magnetic field $B$ and moved with a velocity $v$ perpendicular to the field, the induced emf (called motional emf) across its ends is
$$\varepsilon = Blv$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How can induced emf be produced without varying the magnetic field?
cards.back: The induced emf Blv is called motional emf. Thus, we are able to produce induced emf by moving a conductor instead of varying the magnetic field, that is, by changing the magnetic flux enclosed by the circuit.
cards.quote: The induced emf Blv is called motional emf. Thus, we are able to produce induced emf by moving a conductor instead of varying the magnetic field, that is, by changing the magnetic flux enclosed by the circuit.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In terms of work and charge, what is emf?
cards.back: emf is the work done per unit charge
cards.quote: Since emf is the work done per unit charge

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: To explain induced emf in a stationary conductor, what must we assume about a changing magnetic field?
cards.back: Therefore, to explain the existence of induced emf or induced current, we must assume that a time-varying magnetic field generates an electric field.
cards.quote: Therefore, to explain the existence of induced emf or induced current, we must assume that a time-varying magnetic field generates an electric field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Conversely, a bar magnet in motion (or more generally, a changing magnetic field) can exert a force on the ____.
cards.back: Conversely, a bar magnet in motion (or more generally, a changing magnetic field) can exert a force on the stationary charge.
cards.quote: Conversely, a bar magnet in motion (or more generally, a changing magnetic field) can exert a force on the stationary charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The number of spokes is immaterial because the emf's across the spokes are ____.
cards.back: The number of spokes is immaterial because the emf's across the spokes are in parallel.
cards.quote: The number of spokes is immaterial because the emf's across the spokes are in parallel.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Whether the flux change comes from another coil or from the same coil, how is the flux through a coil related to the current?
cards.back: However, in both the cases, the flux through a coil is proportional to the current.
cards.quote: However, in both the cases, the flux through a coil is proportional to the current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For a closely wound coil of N turns, the ____ is linked with all the turns.
cards.back: For a closely wound coil of N turns, the same magnetic flux is linked with all the turns.
cards.quote: For a closely wound coil of N turns, the same magnetic flux is linked with all the turns.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define inductance.
cards.back: Inductance is the ratio of the flux-linkage to current.
cards.quote: Inductance is the ratio of the flux-linkage to current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: We shall see that inductance depends only on the ____ and intrinsic material properties.
cards.back: We shall see that inductance depends only on the geometry of the coil and intrinsic material properties.
cards.quote: We shall see that inductance depends only on the geometry of the coil and intrinsic material properties.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Is inductance a scalar or a vector quantity?
cards.back: Inductance is a scalar quantity.
cards.quote: Inductance is a scalar quantity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of inductance, and its symbol?
cards.back: The SI unit of inductance is henry and is denoted by H.
cards.quote: The SI unit of inductance is henry and is denoted by H.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In whose honour is the SI unit of inductance named?
cards.back: It is named in honour of Joseph Henry who discovered electromagnetic induction in USA, independently of Faraday in England.
cards.quote: It is named in honour of Joseph Henry who discovered electromagnetic induction in USA, independently of Faraday in England.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: flux linkage N1Φ1 of solenoid S1 due to current I2 in solenoid S2, which defines the mutual inductance M12
cards.back:
When a current I 2 is set up through S2, it in turn sets up a magnetic flux through S1. Let us denote it by Φ1. The corresponding flux linkage with solenoid S 1 is
N 1 Φ1 = MI 12 2
M 12 is called the mutual inductance of solenoid S 1 with respect to solenoid S2. It is also referred to as the coefficient of mutual induction.
cards.quote: When a current I 2 is set up through S2, it in turn sets up a magnetic flux through S1. Let us denote it by Φ1. The corresponding flux linkage with solenoid S 1 is N 1 Φ1 = MI 12 2 (6.7) M 12 is called the mutual inductance of solenoid S 1 with respect to solenoid S2. It is also referred to as the coefficient of mutual induction.

tex.back:
When a current $I_2$ is set up through $S_2$, it in turn sets up a magnetic flux through $S_1$. Let us denote it by $\Phi_1$. The corresponding flux linkage with solenoid $S_1$ is
$$N_1 \Phi_1 = M_{12} I_2$$
$M_{12}$ is called the mutual inductance of solenoid $S_1$ with respect to solenoid $S_2$. It is also referred to as the coefficient of mutual induction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: mutual inductance of two long co-axial solenoids of length l (inner radius r1, n1 and n2 turns per unit length)
cards.back: M 12 = µ0n1n2πr 2l 1
cards.quote: Thus, from Eq. (6.7) and Eq. (6.8), M 12 = µ0n1n2πr 2l 1 (6.9)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How do the mutual inductances M12 and M21 of a pair of coils compare?
cards.back: There exists a general equality, M12 = M21
cards.quote: There exists a general equality, M12 = M21

tex.back: There exists a general equality, $M_{12} = M_{21}$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: mutual inductance of two long co-axial solenoids (length l, inner radius r1, n1 and n2 turns per unit length) with medium μr
cards.back:
Instead, if a medium of relative permeability µr had been present, the mutual inductance would be
M =µr µ0 n1n2π r12 l
cards.quote: Instead, if a medium of relative permeability µr had been present, the mutual inductance would be M =µr µ0 n1n2π r12 l

tex.back:
Instead, if a medium of relative permeability $\mu_r$ had been present, the mutual inductance would be
$$M = \mu_r \mu_0 n_1 n_2 \pi r_1^2 l$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On what two things does the mutual inductance of a pair of coils or solenoids depend?
cards.back: It is also important to know that the mutual inductance of a pair of coils, solenoids, etc., depends on their separation as well as their relative orientation.
cards.quote: It is also important to know that the mutual inductance of a pair of coils, solenoids, etc., depends on their separation as well as their relative orientation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: emf induced in coil 1 by a changing current I2 in a nearby coil 2, with mutual inductance M12
cards.back:
A changing current in a coil (coil 2) can induce an emf in a nearby coil (coil 1). This relation is given by,
ε1 = −M12 dI2 dt
The quantity M12 is called mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2.
cards.quote: A changing current in a coil (coil 2) can induce an emf in a nearby coil (coil 1). This relation is given by, ε1 = −M12 dI2 dt The quantity M12 is called mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2.

tex.back:
A changing current in a coil (coil 2) can induce an emf in a nearby coil (coil 1). This relation is given by,
$$\varepsilon_1 = -M_{12}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}I_2}{\mathrm{d}t}$$
The quantity $M_{12}$ is called mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mutual induction: what can varying current in a coil do, and what does the induced emf depend on?
cards.back: It shows that varying current in a coil can induce emf in a neighbouring coil. The magnitude of the induced emf depends upon the rate of change of current and mutual inductance of the two coils.
cards.quote: It shows that varying current in a coil can induce emf in a neighbouring coil. The magnitude of the induced emf depends upon the rate of change of current and mutual inductance of the two coils.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The magnitude of the induced emf depends upon the ____ and mutual inductance of the two coils.
cards.back: The magnitude of the induced emf depends upon the rate of change of current and mutual inductance of the two coils.
cards.quote: The magnitude of the induced emf depends upon the rate of change of current and mutual inductance of the two coils.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is self-induction?
cards.back: It is also possible that emf is induced in a single isolated coil due to change of flux through the coil by means of varying the current through the same coil. This phenomenon is called self-induction.
cards.quote: It is also possible that emf is induced in a single isolated coil due to change of flux through the coil by means of varying the current through the same coil. This phenomenon is called self-induction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: flux linkage NΦB of a coil of N turns carrying current I, in terms of its self-inductance L
cards.back:
In this case, flux linkage through a coil of N turns is proportional to the current through the coil and is expressed as
NΦB ∝ I
NΦB = L I
cards.quote: In this case, flux linkage through a coil of N turns is proportional to the current through the coil and is expressed as NΦB ∝ I NΦB = L I (6.13)

tex.back:
In this case, flux linkage through a coil of $N$ turns is proportional to the current through the coil and is expressed as
$$N\Phi_B \propto I$$
$$N\Phi_B = L I$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is L, the constant of proportionality between a coil's flux linkage and its current?
cards.back: L is called self-inductance of the coil. It is also called the coefficient of self-induction of the coil.
cards.quote: L is called self-inductance of the coil. It is also called the coefficient of self-induction of the coil.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: emf induced in a coil by a changing current I through the same coil, with self-inductance L
cards.back:
Using Eq. (6.13), the induced emf is given by
ε = – d (NΦB ) dt
dI ε = –L dt
cards.quote: Using Eq. (6.13), the induced emf is given by ε = – d (NΦB ) dt dI ε = –L dt (6.14)

tex.back:
Using Eq. (6.13), the induced emf is given by
$$\varepsilon = -\frac{\mathrm{d}(N\Phi_B)}{\mathrm{d}t}$$
$$\varepsilon = -L\,\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the self-induced emf act on any change (increase or decrease) of current in the coil?
cards.back: Thus, the self-induced emf always opposes any change (increase or decrease) of current in the coil.
cards.quote: Thus, the self-induced emf always opposes any change (increase or decrease) of current in the coil.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: self-inductance of a long solenoid of cross-sectional area A and length l, with n turns per unit length
cards.back:
L = ΝΦΒ I
= µ0n2 Al
cards.quote: Thus, the self-inductance is, L = ΝΦΒ I = µ0n2 Al (6.15)

tex.back:
$$L = \frac{N\Phi_B}{I}$$
$$= \mu_0 n^2 A l$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: self-inductance of a long solenoid with a core of relative permeability μr
cards.back:
The self-inductance of a long solenoid, the core of which consists of a magnetic material of relative permeability mr, is given by
L = mr m0 n2 A l
where A is the area of cross-section of the solenoid, l its length and n the number of turns per unit length.
cards.quote: The self-inductance of a long solenoid, the core of which consists of a magnetic material of relative permeability mr, is given by L = mr m0 n2 A l where A is the area of cross-section of the solenoid, l its length and n the number of turns per unit length.

tex.back:
The self-inductance of a long solenoid, the core of which consists of a magnetic material of relative permeability $\mu_r$, is given by
$$L = \mu_r \mu_0 n^2 A l$$
where $A$ is the area of cross-section of the solenoid, $l$ its length and $n$ the number of turns per unit length.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The self-inductance of the coil depends on its ____ and on the ____ of the medium.
cards.back: The self-inductance of the coil depends on its geometry and on the permeability of the medium.
cards.quote: The self-inductance of the coil depends on its geometry and on the permeability of the medium.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The self-induced emf is also called the ____ as it opposes any change in the current in a circuit.
cards.back: The self-induced emf is also called the back emf as it opposes any change in the current in a circuit.
cards.quote: The self-induced emf is also called the back emf as it opposes any change in the current in a circuit.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Physically, the self-inductance plays the role of ____. It is the electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.
cards.back: Physically, the self-inductance plays the role of inertia. It is the electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.
cards.quote: Physically, the self-inductance plays the role of inertia. It is the electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: energy required to build up a current I in a coil of self-inductance L
cards.back:
Thus, the energy required to build up the current I is,
W = 1 LI 2 2
cards.quote: Thus, the energy required to build up the current I is, W = 1 LI 2 2 (6.17)

tex.back:
Thus, the energy required to build up the current $I$ is,
$$W = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When a current in a coil changes, it induces a back emf in the ____.
cards.back: When a current in a coil changes, it induces a back emf in the same coil.
cards.quote: When a current in a coil changes, it induces a back emf in the same coil.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnetic energy per unit volume in a region where the magnetic field is B
cards.back:
The magnetic energy per unit volume is,
uB = UB V
(where V is volume that contains flux)
= UB Al = B2 2µ0
cards.quote: The magnetic energy per unit volume is, uB = UB V (where V is volume that contains flux) = UB Al = B2 2µ0 (6.18)

tex.back:
The magnetic energy per unit volume is,
$$u_B = \frac{U_B}{V}$$
(where $V$ is volume that contains flux)
$$= \frac{U_B}{Al} = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An exceptionally important application is the generation of ____ (ac).
cards.back: An exceptionally important application is the generation of alternating currents (ac).
cards.quote: An exceptionally important application is the generation of alternating currents (ac).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who is credited with the development of the ac generator?
cards.back: The Yugoslav inventor Nicola Tesla is credited with the development of the machine.
cards.quote: The Yugoslav inventor Nicola Tesla is credited with the development of the machine.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An ac generator converts ____ into electrical energy.
cards.back: An ac generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
cards.quote: An ac generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In an ac generator, what is the coil mounted on, and how is its axis of rotation oriented to the magnetic field?
cards.back: It consists of a coil mounted on a rotor shaft. The axis of rotation of the coil is perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field.
cards.quote: It consists of a coil mounted on a rotor shaft. The axis of rotation of the coil is perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The axis of rotation of the coil is ____ to the direction of the magnetic field.
cards.back: The axis of rotation of the coil is perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field.
cards.quote: The axis of rotation of the coil is perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The coil (called ____) is mechanically rotated in the uniform magnetic field by some external means.
cards.back: The coil (called armature) is mechanically rotated in the uniform magnetic field by some external means.
cards.quote: The coil (called armature) is mechanically rotated in the uniform magnetic field by some external means.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The rotation of the coil causes the ____ through it to change, so an emf is induced in the coil.
cards.back: The rotation of the coil causes the magnetic flux through it to change, so an emf is induced in the coil.
cards.quote: The rotation of the coil causes the magnetic flux through it to change, so an emf is induced in the coil.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The ends of the coil are connected to an external circuit by means of ____.
cards.back: The ends of the coil are connected to an external circuit by means of slip rings and brushes.
cards.quote: The ends of the coil are connected to an external circuit by means of slip rings and brushes.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnetic flux at time t through a coil rotated at constant angular speed ω in a uniform field B, with θ = 0° at t = 0
cards.back:
When the coil is rotated with a constant angular speed w, the angle q between the magnetic field vector B and the area vector A of the coil at any instant t is q = wt (assuming q = 0° at t = 0).
As a result, the effective area of the coil exposed to the magnetic field lines changes with time, and from Eq. (6.1), the flux at any time t is
FB = BA cos q = BA cos wt
cards.quote: When the coil is rotated with a constant angular speed w, the angle q between the magnetic field vector B and the area vector A of the coil at any instant t is q = wt (assuming q = 0° at t = 0). As a result, the effective area of the coil exposed to the magnetic field lines changes with time, and from Eq. (6.1), the flux at any time t is FB = BA cos q = BA cos wt

tex.back:
When the coil is rotated with a constant angular speed $\omega$, the angle $\theta$ between the magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$ and the area vector $\mathbf{A}$ of the coil at any instant $t$ is $\theta = \omega{t}$ (assuming $\theta = 0^\circ$ at $t = 0$).
As a result, the effective area of the coil exposed to the magnetic field lines changes with time, and from Eq. (6.1), the flux at any time $t$ is
$$\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta = BA\cos\omega{t}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: instantaneous emf of an N-turn coil of area A rotating at angular speed ω in a field B, with θ = 0° at t = 0, and its maximum
cards.back:
Thus, the instantaneous value of the emf is
ε = NBA ω sin ωt
where NBAw is the maximum value of the emf, which occurs when sin wt = ±1.
If we denote NBAw as e0, then
e = e0 sin wt
cards.quote: Thus, the instantaneous value of the emf is ε = NBA ω sin ωt (6.19) where NBAw is the maximum value of the emf, which occurs when sin wt = ±1. If we denote NBAw as e0, then e = e0 sin wt

tex.back:
Thus, the instantaneous value of the emf is
$$\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega{t}$$
where $NBA\omega$ is the maximum value of the emf, which occurs when $\sin\omega{t} = \pm 1$.
If we denote $NBA\omega$ as $\varepsilon_0$, then
$$\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0 \sin\omega{t}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In an ac generator coil, at which angles θ between B and A does the emf have its extremum value?
cards.back: Note from Fig. 6.14 that the emf has its extremum value when q = 90° or q = 270°, as the change of flux is greatest at these points.
cards.quote: Note from Fig. 6.14 that the emf has its extremum value when q = 90° or q = 270°, as the change of flux is greatest at these points.

tex.back: Note from Fig. 6.14 that the emf has its extremum value when $\theta = 90^\circ$ or $\theta = 270^\circ$, as the change of flux is greatest at these points.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The direction of the current changes periodically and therefore the current is called ____ (ac).
cards.back: The direction of the current changes periodically and therefore the current is called alternating current (ac).
cards.quote: The direction of the current changes periodically and therefore the current is called alternating current (ac).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Types of commercial generators, by how the armature is made to rotate.
cards.back:
hydro-electric generators
thermal generators
nuclear power generators
cards.quote: In commercial generators, the mechanical energy required for rotation of the armature is provided by water falling from a height, for example, from dams. These are called hydro-electric generators. Alternatively, water is heated to produce steam using coal or other sources. The steam at high pressure produces the rotation of the armature. These are called thermal generators. Instead of coal, if a nuclear fuel is used, we get nuclear power generators.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In most generators, the coils are held stationary and it is the ____ which are rotated.
cards.back: In most generators, the coils are held stationary and it is the electromagnets which are rotated.
cards.quote: In most generators, the coils are held stationary and it is the electromagnets which are rotated.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the frequency of rotation in generators in India, and in the USA?
cards.back: The frequency of rotation is 50 Hz in India. In certain countries such as USA, it is 60 Hz.
cards.quote: The frequency of rotation is 50 Hz in India. In certain countries such as USA, it is 60 Hz.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In an ac generator, mechanical energy is converted to electrical energy by virtue of ____.
cards.back: In an ac generator, mechanical energy is converted to electrical energy by virtue of electromagnetic induction.
cards.quote: In an ac generator, mechanical energy is converted to electrical energy by virtue of electromagnetic induction.

cards.front: Maxwell noticed an ____ in the Ampere's circuital law.
cards.back: Maxwell noticed an inconsistency in the Ampere's circuital law.
cards.quote: Maxwell noticed an inconsistency in the Ampere's circuital law.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: He suggested the existence of an additional current, called by him, the ____ to remove this inconsistency.
cards.back: He suggested the existence of an additional current, called by him, the displacement current to remove this inconsistency.
cards.quote: He suggested the existence of an additional current, called by him, the displacement current to remove this inconsistency.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What, besides an electric current, did Maxwell argue also generates a magnetic field?
cards.back:
A time-varying electric field
not only an electric current but also a time-varying electric field generates magnetic field.
cards.quote: not only an electric current but also a time-varying electric field generates magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are electromagnetic waves (Maxwell's most important prediction)?
cards.back: (coupled) time-varying electric and magnetic fields that propagate in space
cards.quote: The most important prediction to emerge from Maxwell's equations is the existence of electromagnetic waves, which are (coupled) time-varying electric and magnetic fields that propagate in space.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Maxwell concluded that light is which kind of wave?
cards.back: Light is an electromagnetic wave
cards.quote: Light is an electromagnetic wave

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What value of the speed of light, obtained from optical measurements, does NCERT's introduction give?
cards.back: the speed of light( 3 ×108 m/s)
cards.quote: the speed of light( 3 ×108 m/s), obtained from optical measurements.

tex.back: the speed of light ($3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Maxwell's work thus unified the domain of ____.
cards.back: Maxwell's work thus unified the domain of electricity, magnetism and light.
cards.quote: Maxwell's work thus unified the domain of electricity, magnetism and light.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Maxwell showed that for logical consistency, a ____ must also produce a magnetic field.
cards.back: Maxwell showed that for logical consistency, a changing electric field must also produce a magnetic field.
cards.quote: Maxwell showed that for logical consistency, a changing electric field must also produce a magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which effect explains the existence of radio waves, gamma rays, visible light and all other electromagnetic waves?
cards.back:
A changing electric field produces a magnetic field
Maxwell showed that for logical consistency, a changing electric field must also produce a magnetic field. This effect is of great importance because it explains the existence of radio waves, gamma rays and visible light, as well as all other forms of electromagnetic waves.
cards.quote: Maxwell showed that for logical consistency, a changing electric field must also produce a magnetic field. This effect is of great importance because it explains the existence of radio waves, gamma rays and visible light, as well as all other forms of electromagnetic waves.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: Ampere's circuital law (Eq. 8.1), before Maxwell adds the displacement current
cards.back:
Ampere’s circuital law given by (Chapter 4)
“B.dl = m0 i (t )
cards.quote: Ampere’s circuital law given by (Chapter 4) “B.dl = m0 i (t ) (8.1)

tex.back:
Ampere’s circuital law given by (Chapter 4)
$$\oint \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} = \mu_0\, i(t)$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnitude of the electric field between the plates of a capacitor of plate area A and charge Q
cards.back: the magnitude of the electric field E between the plates is (Q/A)/e0
cards.quote: the magnitude of the electric field E between the plates is (Q/A)/e0 (see Eq. 2.41).

tex.back: the magnitude of the electric field $\mathbf{E}$ between the plates is $(Q/A)/\varepsilon_0$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: electric flux through the surface S between the capacitor plates (Gauss's law, charge Q, area A)
cards.back:
Using Gauss’s law, it is
ΦE = E A = 1 ε0 Q A A = Q ε0
cards.quote: Using Gauss’s law, it is ΦE = E A = 1 ε0 Q A A = Q ε0 (8.3)

tex.back:
Using Gauss’s law, it is
$$\Phi_E = |\mathbf{E}|A = \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{Q}{A}\,A = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: total current i as the sum of the conduction current and the displacement current
cards.back:
the total current i is the sum of the conduction current denoted by ic, and the displacement current denoted by id
i = i c + id =ic + ε0 dΦE dt
cards.quote: the total current i is the sum of the conduction current denoted by ic, and the displacement current denoted by id (= ✒ 0 (d✂E/dt)). So we have i = i c + id =ic + ε0 dΦE dt (8.5)

tex.back:
the total current $i$ is the sum of the conduction current denoted by $i_c$, and the displacement current denoted by $i_d$
$$i = i_c + i_d = i_c + \varepsilon_0 \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_E}{\mathrm{d}t}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: "the total current passing through any surface of which the closed loop is the perimeter" is the sum of the ____ and the ____.
cards.back: "the total current passing through any surface of which the closed loop is the perimeter" is the sum of the conduction current and the displacement current.
cards.quote: "the total current passing through any surface of which the closed loop is the perimeter" is the sum of the conduction current and the displacement current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the generalised Ampere's circuital law (with displacement current) known as?
cards.back: Ampere-Maxwell law
cards.quote: and is known as Ampere-Maxwell law.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In all respects, the displacement current has ____ as the conduction current.
cards.back: In all respects, the displacement current has the same physical effects as the conduction current.
cards.quote: In all respects, the displacement current has the same physical effects as the conduction current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In some cases, for example, ____ in a conducting wire, the displacement current may be zero since the electric field E does not change with time.
cards.back: In some cases, for example, steady electric fields in a conducting wire, the displacement current may be zero since the electric field E does not change with time.
cards.quote: In some cases, for example, steady electric fields in a conducting wire, the displacement current may be zero since the electric field E does not change with time.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Most interestingly, there may be large regions of space where there is no conduction current, but there is ____ due to time-varying electric fields.
cards.back: Most interestingly, there may be large regions of space where there is no conduction current, but there is only a displacement current due to time-varying electric fields.
cards.quote: Most interestingly, there may be large regions of space where there is no conduction current, but there is only a displacement current due to time-varying electric fields.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In such a region, we expect a ____, though there is no (conduction) current source nearby!
cards.back: In such a region, we expect a magnetic field, though there is no (conduction) current source nearby!
cards.quote: In such a region, we expect a magnetic field, though there is no (conduction) current source nearby!

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Faraday's law of induction states that there is an induced emf equal to the ____.
cards.back: Faraday's law of induction states that there is an induced emf equal to the rate of change of magnetic flux.
cards.quote: Faraday's law of induction states that there is an induced emf equal to the rate of change of magnetic flux.
blanks: rate of change of magnetic flux

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How can Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction be rephrased in terms of fields?
cards.back:
A changing magnetic field gives rise to an electric field
So, we can rephrase Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction by saying that a magnetic field, changing with time, gives rise to an electric field.
cards.quote: So, we can rephrase Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction by saying that a magnetic field, changing with time, gives rise to an electric field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the mutual relation between time-dependent electric and magnetic fields?
cards.back:
They give rise to each other
Thus, time-dependent electric and magnetic fields give rise to each other!
cards.quote: Thus, time-dependent electric and magnetic fields give rise to each other!

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: One very important consequence of this symmetry is the ____, which we discuss qualitatively in the next section.
cards.back: One very important consequence of this symmetry is the existence of electromagnetic waves, which we discuss qualitatively in the next section.
cards.quote: One very important consequence of this symmetry is the existence of electromagnetic waves, which we discuss qualitatively in the next section.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: Maxwell's equation in vacuum for Gauss's law for magnetism
cards.back:
“B.dA = 0
(Gauss’s Law for magnetism)
cards.quote: 2. “B.dA = 0 (Gauss’s Law for magnetism)

tex.back:
$$\oint \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{A} = 0$$
(Gauss’s Law for magnetism)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: Maxwell's equation in vacuum for Faraday's law
cards.back:
“E.dl = –d d ΦB t

tex.back:
$$\oint \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} = \frac{-\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t}$$
(Faraday’s Law)

cards.back: “B.dl = d d µ µ ε 0 0 0 i t c E + Φ

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Neither ____ nor ____ (steady currents) can be sources of electromagnetic waves.
cards.back: Neither stationary charges nor charges in uniform motion (steady currents) can be sources of electromagnetic waves.
cards.quote: Neither stationary charges nor charges in uniform motion (steady currents) can be sources of electromagnetic waves.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why cannot stationary charges or steady currents give electromagnetic waves?
cards.back: Neither stationary charges nor charges in uniform motion (steady currents) can be sources of electromagnetic waves. The former produces only electrostatic fields, while the latter produces magnetic fields that, however, do not vary with time.
cards.quote: Neither stationary charges nor charges in uniform motion (steady currents) can be sources of electromagnetic waves. The former produces only electrostatic fields, while the latter produces magnetic fields that, however, do not vary with time.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: According to Maxwell's theory, which charges radiate electromagnetic waves?
cards.back:
Accelerated charges
It is an important result of Maxwell's theory that accelerated charges radiate electromagnetic waves.
cards.quote: It is an important result of Maxwell's theory that accelerated charges radiate electromagnetic waves.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The oscillating electric and magnetic fields thus ____, so to speak, as the wave propagates through the space.
cards.back: The oscillating electric and magnetic fields thus regenerate each other, so to speak, as the wave propagates through the space.
cards.quote: The oscillating electric and magnetic fields thus regenerate each other, so to speak, as the wave propagates through the space.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The frequency of the electromagnetic wave naturally equals the ____.
cards.back: The frequency of the electromagnetic wave naturally equals the frequency of oscillation of the charge.
cards.quote: The frequency of the electromagnetic wave naturally equals the frequency of oscillation of the charge.
blanks: frequency of oscillation of the charge

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How are the electric and magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave oriented?
cards.back:
Perpendicular to each other, and to the direction of propagation
It can be shown from Maxwell's equations that electric and magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave are perpendicular to each other, and to the direction of propagation.
cards.quote: It can be shown from Maxwell's equations that electric and magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave are perpendicular to each other, and to the direction of propagation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: electric and magnetic fields of a plane electromagnetic wave travelling along the z direction
cards.back:
We can write Ex and By as follows:
Ex= E0 sin (kz–wt )
By= B0 sin (kz–wt )
cards.quote: We can write Ex and By as follows: Ex= E0 sin (kz–wt ) [8.7(a)] By= B0 sin (kz–wt ) [8.7(b)]

tex.back:
We can write $E_x$ and $B_y$ as follows:
$$E_x = E_0 \sin(kz - \omega t)$$
$$B_y = B_0 \sin(kz - \omega t)$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: wave number k of an electromagnetic wave in terms of its wavelength λ
cards.back:
Here k is related to the wave length l of the wave by the usual equation
2 k λ π =
cards.quote: Here k is related to the wave length l of the wave by the usual equation 2 k λ π = (8.8)

tex.back:
Here $k$ is related to the wave length $\lambda$ of the wave by the usual equation
$$k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electric and magnetic fields oscillate ____ in space and time in an electromagnetic wave.
cards.back: Electric and magnetic fields oscillate sinusoidally in space and time in an electromagnetic wave.
cards.quote: Electric and magnetic fields oscillate sinusoidally in space and time in an electromagnetic wave.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: relation between the angular frequency ω, the wave number k and the speed c of an electromagnetic wave
cards.back:
The speed of propagation of the wave is (ω/k ).
The relation ω = ck is the standard one for waves
cards.quote: The speed of propagation of the wave is (ω/k ). Using Eqs. [8.7(a) and (b)] for Ex and By and Maxwell’s equations, one finds that ω = ck, where, c = 1/ µ0ε0 [8.9(a)] The relation ω = ck is the standard one for waves

tex.back:
The speed of propagation of the wave is $(\omega/k)$.
The relation $\omega = ck$ is the standard one for waves

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: relation between the frequency ν, the wavelength λ and the speed c of an electromagnetic wave
cards.back:
This relation is often written in terms of frequency, ν (=ω/2π) and wavelength, λ (=2π/k) as
2πν = c 2π λ or νλ = c
cards.quote: This relation is often written in terms of frequency, ν (=ω/2π) and wavelength, λ (=2π/k) as 2πν = c 2π λ or νλ = c [8.9(b)]

tex.back:
This relation is often written in terms of frequency, $
u\ (=\omega/2\pi)$ and wavelength, $\lambda\ (=2\pi/k)$ as
$2\pi
u = c\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}ight)$ or $
u\lambda = c$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: relation between the magnetic field amplitude B₀ and the electric field amplitude E₀ in an electromagnetic wave
cards.back:
the magnitude of the electric and the magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave are related as
B0 = (E0/c)
cards.quote: the magnitude of the electric and the magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave are related as B0 = (E0/c) (8.10)

tex.back:
the magnitude of the electric and the magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave are related as
$$B_0 = (E_0/c)$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are electromagnetic waves, in terms of oscillations of fields?
cards.back: They are self-sustaining oscillations of electric and magnetic fields in free space, or vacuum.
cards.quote: They are self-sustaining oscillations of electric and magnetic fields in free space, or vacuum.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electromagnetic waves differ from all other waves studied so far in what respect about a medium?
cards.back:
No material medium is involved in the vibrations
They differ from all the other waves we have studied so far, in respect that no material medium is involved in the vibrations of the electric and magnetic fields.
cards.quote: They differ from all the other waves we have studied so far, in respect that no material medium is involved in the vibrations of the electric and magnetic fields.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On what does the velocity of light in a material medium depend?
cards.back:
The electric and magnetic properties of the medium
Thus, the velocity of light depends on electric and magnetic properties of the medium.
cards.quote: Thus, the velocity of light depends on electric and magnetic properties of the medium.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The velocity of electromagnetic waves in free space or vacuum is an important ____.
cards.back: The velocity of electromagnetic waves in free space or vacuum is an important fundamental constant.
cards.quote: The velocity of electromagnetic waves in free space or vacuum is an important fundamental constant.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the velocity of em waves in vacuum depend on wavelength?
cards.back: this velocity is the same (independent of wavelength) to within a few metres per second
cards.quote: It has been shown by experiments on electromagnetic waves of different wavelengths that this velocity is the same (independent of wavelength) to within a few metres per second

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The great technological importance of electromagnetic waves stems from their capability to ____ from one place to another.
cards.back: The great technological importance of electromagnetic waves stems from their capability to carry energy from one place to another.
cards.quote: The great technological importance of electromagnetic waves stems from their capability to carry energy from one place to another.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: speed c of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum in terms of μ₀ and ε₀
cards.back:
The speed c of electromagnetic wave in vacuum is related to m0 and e0 (the free space permeability and permittivity constants) as follows:
c = 1/ µ0 ε0
cards.quote: The speed c of electromagnetic wave in vacuum is related to m0 and e0 (the free space permeability and permittivity constants) as follows: c = 1/ µ0 ε0

tex.back:
The speed $c$ of electromagnetic wave in vacuum is related to $\mu_0$ and $\varepsilon_0$ (the free space permeability and permittivity constants) as follows:
$$c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electromagnetic waves other than light also have ____ in free space.
cards.back: Electromagnetic waves other than light also have the same velocity c in free space.
cards.quote: Electromagnetic waves other than light also have the same velocity c in free space.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: speed of light, or of electromagnetic waves, in a material medium of permeability μ and permittivity ε
cards.back:
The speed of light, or of electromagnetic waves in a material medium is given by
v = 1/ µ ε
where m is the permeability of the medium and e its permittivity.
cards.quote: The speed of light, or of electromagnetic waves in a material medium is given by v = 1/ µ ε where m is the permeability of the medium and e its permittivity.

tex.back:
The speed of light, or of electromagnetic waves in a material medium is given by
$$v = 1/\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$$
where $\mu$ is the permeability of the medium and $\varepsilon$ its permittivity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Name the kinds of electromagnetic waves.
cards.back:
visible light waves
X-rays
gamma rays
radio waves
microwaves
ultraviolet and infrared waves
cards.quote: We now know that, electromagnetic waves include visible light waves, X-rays, gamma rays, radio waves, microwaves, ultraviolet and infrared waves.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The classification of em waves according to frequency is the ____ (Fig. 8.4).
cards.back: The classification of em waves according to frequency is the electromagnetic spectrum (Fig. 8.4).
cards.quote: The classification of em waves according to frequency is the electromagnetic spectrum (Fig. 8.4).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: There is ____ between one kind of wave and the next.
cards.back: There is no sharp division between one kind of wave and the next.
cards.quote: There is no sharp division between one kind of wave and the next.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The classification is based roughly on how the waves are ____.
cards.back: The classification is based roughly on how the waves are produced and/or detected.
cards.quote: The classification is based roughly on how the waves are produced and/or detected.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The spectrum of electromagnetic waves stretches, in principle, over an ____.
cards.back: The spectrum of electromagnetic waves stretches, in principle, over an infinite range of wavelengths.
cards.quote: The spectrum of electromagnetic waves stretches, in principle, over an infinite range of wavelengths.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Steps: regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing wavelength, and the range they cover
cards.back:
g-rays
X-rays
ultraviolet rays
visible rays
infrared rays
microwaves
radio waves
from 10–2 Å or 10–12 m to 106 m
cards.quote: g-rays, X-rays, ultraviolet rays, visible rays, infrared rays, microwaves and radio waves in order of increasing wavelength from 10–2 Å or 10–12 m to 106 m.

tex.back:
$\gamma$-rays
X-rays
ultraviolet rays
visible rays
infrared rays
microwaves
radio waves
from $10^{-2}\ \text{Å}$ or $10^{-12}\ \text{m}$ to $10^{6}\ \text{m}$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Radio waves are used in which communication systems?
cards.back: radio and television communication systems
cards.quote: They are used in radio and television communication systems.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the general frequency range of radio waves?
cards.back:
500 kHz to about 1000 MHz
They are generally in the frequency range from 500 kHz to about 1000 MHz.
cards.quote: They are generally in the frequency range from 500 kHz to about 1000 MHz.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The AM (amplitude modulated) band is from ____ to ____.
cards.back: The AM (amplitude modulated) band is from 530 kHz to 1710 kHz.
cards.quote: The AM (amplitude modulated) band is from 530 kHz to 1710 kHz.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: TV waves range from 54 MHz to ____.
cards.back: TV waves range from 54 MHz to 890 MHz.
cards.quote: TV waves range from 54 MHz to 890 MHz.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The FM (frequency modulated) radio band extends from ____ to ____.
cards.back: The FM (frequency modulated) radio band extends from 88 MHz to 108 MHz.
cards.quote: The FM (frequency modulated) radio band extends from 88 MHz to 108 MHz.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Cellular phones use radio waves to transmit voice communication in the ____ band.
cards.back: Cellular phones use radio waves to transmit voice communication in the ultrahigh frequency (UHF) band.
cards.quote: Cellular phones use radio waves to transmit voice communication in the ultrahigh frequency (UHF) band.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How are microwaves produced?
cards.back: by special vacuum tubes (called klystrons, magnetrons and Gunn diodes)
cards.quote: Microwaves (short-wavelength radio waves), with frequencies in the gigahertz (GHz) range, are produced by special vacuum tubes (called klystrons, magnetrons and Gunn diodes).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Due to their short wavelengths, they are suitable for the ____ used in aircraft navigation.
cards.back: Due to their short wavelengths, they are suitable for the radar systems used in aircraft navigation.
cards.quote: Due to their short wavelengths, they are suitable for the radar systems used in aircraft navigation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Infrared waves are sometimes referred to as ____.
cards.back: Infrared waves are sometimes referred to as heat waves.
cards.quote: Infrared waves are sometimes referred to as heat waves.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why are infrared waves sometimes referred to as heat waves?
cards.back:
Water molecules present in most materials readily absorb them
Infrared waves are sometimes referred to as heat waves. This is because water molecules present in most materials readily absorb infrared waves
cards.quote: Infrared waves are sometimes referred to as heat waves. This is because water molecules present in most materials readily absorb infrared waves

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where does the band of infrared waves lie with respect to the visible spectrum?
cards.back:
Adjacent to the low-frequency or long-wave length end
Infrared waves are produced by hot bodies and molecules. This band lies adjacent to the low-frequency or long-wave length end of the visible spectrum.
cards.quote: Infrared waves are produced by hot bodies and molecules. This band lies adjacent to the low-frequency or long-wave length end of the visible spectrum.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Infrared lamps are used in ____.
cards.back: Infrared lamps are used in physical therapy.
cards.quote: Infrared lamps are used in physical therapy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Infrared radiation also plays an important role in maintaining the earth's warmth or average temperature through the ____.
cards.back: Infrared radiation also plays an important role in maintaining the earth's warmth or average temperature through the greenhouse effect.
cards.quote: Infrared radiation also plays an important role in maintaining the earth's warmth or average temperature through the greenhouse effect.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: By what is the infrared radiation re-radiated from the earth's surface trapped?
cards.back:
Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour
Incoming visible light (which passes relatively easily through the atmosphere) is absorbed by the earth's surface and re-radiated as infrared (longer wavelength) radiations. This radiation is trapped by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour.
cards.quote: Incoming visible light (which passes relatively easily through the atmosphere) is absorbed by the earth's surface and re-radiated as infrared (longer wavelength) radiations. This radiation is trapped by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Infrared detectors are used in Earth satellites, both for military purposes and to observe ____.
cards.back: Infrared detectors are used in Earth satellites, both for military purposes and to observe growth of crops.
cards.quote: Infrared detectors are used in Earth satellites, both for military purposes and to observe growth of crops.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which household devices use infrared from light emitting diodes?
cards.back: the remote switches of household electronic systems such as TV sets, video recorders and hi-fi systems
cards.quote: Electronic devices (for example semiconductor light emitting diodes) also emit infrared and are widely used in the remote switches of household electronic systems such as TV sets, video recorders and hi-fi systems.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Over what range of frequencies does visible light run, according to NCERT?
cards.back: about 4 × 1014 Hz to about 7 × 1014 Hz
cards.quote: It runs from about 4 × 1014 Hz to about 7 × 1014 Hz

tex.back: about $4 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$ to about $7 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Exposure to UV radiation induces the production of more ____, causing tanning of the skin.
cards.back: Exposure to UV radiation induces the production of more melanin, causing tanning of the skin.
cards.quote: Exposure to UV radiation induces the production of more melanin, causing tanning of the skin.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: UV radiation is absorbed by ____. Hence, one cannot get tanned or sunburn through glass windows.
cards.back: UV radiation is absorbed by ordinary glass. Hence, one cannot get tanned or sunburn through glass windows.
cards.quote: UV radiation is absorbed by ordinary glass. Hence, one cannot get tanned or sunburn through glass windows.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Welders wear special glass goggles or face masks with glass windows to protect their eyes from large amount of UV produced by ____.
cards.back: Welders wear special glass goggles or face masks with glass windows to protect their eyes from large amount of UV produced by welding arcs.
cards.quote: Welders wear special glass goggles or face masks with glass windows to protect their eyes from large amount of UV produced by welding arcs.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: UV lamps are used to kill germs in ____.
cards.back: UV lamps are used to kill germs in water purifiers.
cards.quote: UV lamps are used to kill germs in water purifiers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: One common way to generate X-rays is to bombard a ____ by high energy electrons.
cards.back: One common way to generate X-rays is to bombard a metal target by high energy electrons.
cards.quote: One common way to generate X-rays is to bombard a metal target by high energy electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: X-rays are used as a ____ in medicine and as a treatment for certain forms of cancer.
cards.back: X-rays are used as a diagnostic tool in medicine and as a treatment for certain forms of cancer.
cards.quote: X-rays are used as a diagnostic tool in medicine and as a treatment for certain forms of cancer.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Because X-rays ____ and organisms, care must be taken to avoid unnecessary or over exposure.
cards.back: Because X-rays damage or destroy living tissues and organisms, care must be taken to avoid unnecessary or over exposure.
cards.quote: Because X-rays damage or destroy living tissues and organisms, care must be taken to avoid unnecessary or over exposure.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In which frequency range of the electromagnetic spectrum do gamma rays lie?
cards.back:
In the upper frequency range
They lie in the upper frequency range of the electromagnetic spectrum
cards.quote: They lie in the upper frequency range of the electromagnetic spectrum

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is gamma radiation produced, and what also emits it?
cards.back:
Produced in nuclear reactions; also emitted by radioactive nuclei
This high frequency radiation is produced in nuclear reactions and also emitted by radioactive nuclei.
cards.quote: This high frequency radiation is produced in nuclear reactions and also emitted by radioactive nuclei.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are gamma rays used for in medicine?
cards.back:
To destroy cancer cells
They are used in medicine to destroy cancer cells.
cards.quote: They are used in medicine to destroy cancer cells.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Table 8.1: how are radio waves produced?
cards.back: Rapid acceleration and decelerations of electrons in aerials
cards.quote: Rapid acceleration and decelerations of electrons in aerials

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On what does the work done by an electrostatic field in moving a charge between two points depend?
cards.back: It means that the work done by an electrostatic field in moving a charge from one point to another depends only on the initial and the final points and is independent of the path taken to go from one point to the other.
cards.quote: It means that the work done by an electrostatic field in moving a charge from one point to another depends only on the initial and the final points and is independent of the path taken to go from one point to the other.
cards.note: Path independence is the fundamental characteristic of a conservative force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define electric potential energy difference between two points.
cards.back: Therefore, we can define electric potential energy difference between two points as the work required to be done by an external force in moving (without accelerating) charge q from one point to another for electric field of any arbitrary charge configuration.
cards.quote: Therefore, we can define electric potential energy difference between two points as the work required to be done by an external force in moving (without accelerating) charge q from one point to another for electric field of any arbitrary charge configuration.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: potential energy difference ΔU between points R and P, in terms of the work W done by the external force.
cards.back:
Thus, potential energy difference
∆U = U P − U R = WRP
cards.quote: Thus, potential energy difference ∆U = U P − U R = WRP

tex.back:
Thus, potential energy difference
$$\Delta U = U_P - U_R = W_{RP}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which quantity of potential energy is physically significant, given that its actual value is not?
cards.back: the actual value of potential energy is not physically significant; it is only the difference of potential energy that is significant.
cards.quote: the actual value of potential energy is not physically significant; it is only the difference of potential energy that is significant.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A convenient choice is to have electrostatic potential energy zero at ____.
cards.back: A convenient choice is to have electrostatic potential energy zero at infinity.
cards.quote: A convenient choice is to have electrostatic potential energy zero at infinity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the potential energy of a charge q at a point in an electric field.
cards.back: Potential energy of charge q at a point (in the presence of field due to any charge configuration) is the work done by the external force (equal and opposite to the electric force) in bringing the charge q from infinity to that point.
cards.quote: Potential energy of charge q at a point (in the presence of field due to any charge configuration) is the work done by the external force (equal and opposite to the electric force) in bringing the charge q from infinity to that point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the electrostatic potential at a point in an electrostatic field.
cards.back: In other words, the electrostatic potential (V) at any point in a region with electrostatic field is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge (without acceleration) from infinity to that point.
cards.quote: In other words, the electrostatic potential (V) at any point in a region with electrostatic field is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge (without acceleration) from infinity to that point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from R to P, in terms of the potentials VP, VR and the potential energies.
cards.back:
Work done by external force in bringing a unit positive charge from point R to P
= VP – VR = − U U q P R
cards.quote: Work done by external force in bringing a unit positive charge from point R to P = VP – VR = − U U q P R

tex.back:
Work done by external force in bringing a unit positive charge from point R to P
$$= V_P - V_R \quad \left(= \frac{U_P - U_R}{q}\right)$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Note, as before, that it is not the actual value of potential but the ____ that is physically significant.
cards.back: Note, as before, that it is not the actual value of potential but the potential difference that is physically significant.
cards.quote: Note, as before, that it is not the actual value of potential but the potential difference that is physically significant.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: electrostatic potential V(r) due to a point charge Q at the origin, at distance r.
cards.back:
This, by definition is the potential at P due to the charge Q
V (r ) = Q 4πε0r
cards.quote: This, by definition is the potential at P due to the charge Q (2.7) 48 V (r ) = Q 4πε0r

tex.back:
This, by definition is the potential at P due to the charge $Q$
$$V(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$

cards.front: Since potential is related to the work done by the field, electrostatic potential also follows the ____ principle.
cards.back: Since potential is related to the work done by the field, electrostatic potential also follows the superposition principle.
cards.quote: Since potential is related to the work done by the field, electrostatic potential also follows the superposition principle.

source.section: Potential due to an Electric Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: electric potential V of a dipole of moment p at position vector r (r much greater than a).
cards.back:
The electric potential of a dipole is then given by
V = 1 4πε0 p.rˆ r2 ; (r >> a)
cards.quote: The electric potential of a dipole is then given by V = 1 4πε0 p.rˆ r2 ; (r >> a)

tex.back:
The electric potential of a dipole is then given by
$$V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\mathbf{p}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{r}}}{r^{2}}; \quad (r \gg a)$$

source.section: Potential due to an Electric Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: potential on the axis of a dipole of moment p, and its value in the equatorial plane.
cards.back:
From Eq. (2.15), potential on the dipole axis (q = 0, p ) is given by
V = ±1 4πε0 p r2
(Positive sign for q = 0, negative sign for q = p.)
The potential in the equatorial plane (q = p/2) is zero.
cards.quote: From Eq. (2.15), potential on the dipole axis (q = 0, p ) is given by V = ±1 4πε0 p r2 (2.16) (Positive sign for q = 0, negative sign for q = p.) The potential in the equatorial plane (q = p/2) is zero.

tex.back:
From Eq. (2.15), potential on the dipole axis $(\theta = 0, \pi)$ is given by
$$V = \pm\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p}{r^{2}}$$
(Positive sign for $\theta = 0$, negative sign for $\theta = \pi$.)
The potential in the equatorial plane $(\theta = \pi/2)$ is zero.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: At large distance, how does the potential of an electric dipole fall off with r, compared with that of a single charge?
cards.back: The electric dipole potential falls off, at large distance, as 1/r 2, not as 1/r, characteristic of the potential due to a single charge.
cards.quote: The electric dipole potential falls off, at large distance, as 1/r 2, not as 1/r, characteristic of the potential due to a single charge.

tex.back: The electric dipole potential falls off, at large distance, as $1/r^{2}$, not as $1/r$, characteristic of the potential due to a single charge.

cards.front: Besides the distance r, what else does the potential due to a dipole depend on?
cards.back: The potential due to a dipole depends not just on r but also on the angle between the position vector r and the dipole moment vector p.
cards.quote: The potential due to a dipole depends not just on r but also on the angle between the position vector r and the dipole moment vector p.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: By the superposition principle, how is the potential at P due to a system of charges obtained?
cards.back: By the superposition principle, the potential V at P due to the total charge configuration is the algebraic sum of the potentials due to the individual charges
cards.quote: By the superposition principle, the potential V at P due to the total charge configuration is the algebraic sum of the potentials due to the individual charges

source.section: Potential due to a System of Charges

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: potential at a point P due to charges q1, q2, ..., qn, by the superposition principle.
cards.back:
For a charge configuration q1, q2, ..., qn with position vectors r1, r2, ... rn, the potential at a point P is given by the superposition principle
V = 1 ( q1 4πε0 r1P + q2 r2P + ... + qn ) rnP
where r1P is the distance between q1 and P, as and so on.
cards.quote: For a charge configuration q1, q2, ..., qn with position vectors r1, r2, ... rn, the potential at a point P is given by the superposition principle V = 1 ( q1 4πε0 r1P + q2 r2P + ... + qn ) rnP where r1P is the distance between q1 and P, as and so on.

tex.back:
For a charge configuration $q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_n$ with position vectors $\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{r}_n$, the potential at a point P is given by the superposition principle
$$V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{q_1}{r_{1P}} + \frac{q_2}{r_{2P}} + \ldots + \frac{q_n}{r_{nP}}\right)$$
where $r_{1P}$ is the distance between $q_1$ and P, as and so on.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Uniformly charged spherical shell: what is the potential inside the shell?
cards.back: The electric field inside the shell is zero. This implies (Section 2.6) that potential is constant inside the shell (as no work is done in moving a charge inside the shell), and, therefore, equals its value at the surface
cards.quote: The electric field inside the shell is zero. This implies (Section 2.6) that potential is constant inside the shell (as no work is done in moving a charge inside the shell), and, therefore, equals its value at the surface

source.section: Potential due to a System of Charges

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: potential V of a uniformly charged spherical shell (charge q, radius R) outside it, and on and inside it.
cards.back:
Thus, the potential outside the shell is given by
V = 1 4πε0 q r (r ≥ R)
where q is the total charge on the shell and R its radius.
The electric field inside the shell is zero. This implies (Section 2.6) that potential is constant inside the shell (as no work is done in moving a charge inside the shell), and, therefore, equals its value at the surface, which is
V= 1 q 4πε0 R
cards.quote: Thus, the potential outside the shell is given by V = 1 4πε0 q r (r ≥ R) [2.19(a)] where q is the total charge on the shell and R its radius. The electric field inside the shell is zero. This implies (Section 2.6) that potential is constant inside the shell (as no work is done in moving a charge inside the shell), and, therefore, equals its value at the surface, which is V= 1 q 4πε0 R

tex.back:
Thus, the potential outside the shell is given by
$$V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r} \quad (r \ge R)$$
where $q$ is the total charge on the shell and $R$ its radius.
The electric field inside the shell is zero. This implies (Section 2.6) that potential is constant inside the shell (as no work is done in moving a charge inside the shell), and, therefore, equals its value at the surface, which is
$$V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{R}$$

source.section: Potential due to a System of Charges

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define an equipotential surface.
cards.back: An equipotential surface is a surface with a constant value of potential at all points on the surface.
cards.quote: An equipotential surface is a surface with a constant value of potential at all points on the surface.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What do the equipotential surfaces of a single point charge look like?
cards.back: Thus, equipotential surfaces of a single point charge are concentric spherical surfaces centred at the charge.
cards.quote: Thus, equipotential surfaces of a single point charge are concentric spherical surfaces centred at the charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is the equipotential surface through a point oriented relative to the electric field at that point?
cards.back: This is true in general: for any charge configuration, equipotential surface through a point is normal to the electric field at that point.
cards.quote: This is true in general: for any charge configuration, equipotential surface through a point is normal to the electric field at that point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What do we know about the potential difference between any two points on an equipotential surface?
cards.back: there is no potential difference between any two points on the surface and no work is required to move a test charge on the surface.
cards.quote: there is no potential difference between any two points on the surface and no work is required to move a test charge on the surface.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the equipotential surfaces for a uniform electric field along the x-axis?
cards.back: For a uniform electric field E, say, along the x-axis, the equipotential surfaces are planes normal to the x-axis, i.e., planes parallel to the y-z plane
cards.quote: For a uniform electric field E, say, along the x-axis, the equipotential surfaces are planes normal to the x-axis, i.e., planes parallel to the y-z plane

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In which direction does the electric field point with respect to the potential?
cards.back: Electric field is in the direction in which the potential decreases steepest.
cards.quote: Electric field is in the direction in which the potential decreases steepest.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is the magnitude of the electric field related to the potential?
cards.back: Its magnitude is given by the change in the magnitude of potential per unit displacement normal to the equipotential surface at the point.
cards.quote: Its magnitude is given by the change in the magnitude of potential per unit displacement normal to the equipotential surface at the point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnitude |E| of the electric field in terms of the potential change δV over the perpendicular distance δl.
cards.back:
Thus, |E|d l = V – (V + dV )= – dV
i.e., |E|= − δV δl
cards.quote: Thus, |E|d l = V – (V + dV )= – dV i.e., |E|= − δV δl

tex.back:
Thus, $|\mathbf{E}|\,\delta l = V - (V + \delta V) = -\delta V$
i.e., $|\mathbf{E}| = -\frac{\delta V}{\delta l}$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the potential energy stored in a system of charges.
cards.back: Potential energy stored in a system of charges is the work done (by an external agency) in assembling the charges at their locations.
cards.quote: Potential energy stored in a system of charges is the work done (by an external agency) in assembling the charges at their locations.

source.section: Potential Energy of a System of Charges

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: potential energy U of two point charges q1 and q2 a distance r12 apart.
cards.back:
Potential energy of two charges q1, q2 at r1, r2 is given by
U = 1 q1 q2 4πε0 r12
where r12 is distance between q1 and q2.
cards.quote: Potential energy of two charges q1, q2 at r1, r2 is given by U = 1 q1 q2 4πε0 r12 where r12 is distance between q1 and q2.

tex.back:
Potential energy of two charges $q_1$, $q_2$ at $\mathbf{r}_1$, $\mathbf{r}_2$ is given by
$$U = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}}$$
where $r_{12}$ is distance between $q_1$ and $q_2$.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For a system of two charges q1 and q2, when is the potential energy positive?
cards.back: If q1q2 > 0, potential energy is positive.
cards.quote: If q1q2 > 0, potential energy is positive.

source.section: Potential Energy of a System of Charges

cards.note: q1q2 > 0 means like charges; the force between them is repulsive.

tex.back: If $q_1 q_2 > 0$, potential energy is positive.
tex.front: For a system of two charges $q_1$ and $q_2$, when is the potential energy positive?

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: potential energy U of three point charges q1, q2, q3 with distances r12, r13, r23 between them.
cards.back: U = 1 4πε0 q1q2 r12 + q1q3 r13 + q2q3 r23
cards.quote: U = 1 4πε0 q1q2 r12 + q1q3 r13 + q2q3 r23

tex.back: $$U = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}} + \frac{q_1 q_3}{r_{13}} + \frac{q_2 q_3}{r_{23}}\right)$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the work done in bringing a charge q from infinity to a point P in an external field, and where is it stored?
cards.back: Thus, work done in bringing a charge q from infinity to the point P in the external field is qV. This work is stored in the form of potential energy of q.
cards.quote: Thus, work done in bringing a charge q from infinity to the point P in the external field is qV. This work is stored in the form of potential energy of q.

source.section: Potential Energy in an External Field

cards.note: V is the external potential at P.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define 1 electron volt (1 eV) and give its value in joules.
cards.back:
Thus, if an electron with charge q = e = 1.6×10–19 C is accelerated by a potential difference of DV = 1 volt, it would gain energy of qDV = 1.6 × 10–19J.
This unit of energy is defined as 1 electron volt or 1eV, i.e., 1 eV=1.6 × 10–19J.
cards.quote: Thus, if an electron with charge q = e = 1.6×10–19 C is accelerated by a potential difference of DV = 1 volt, it would gain energy of qDV = 1.6 × 10–19J. This unit of energy is defined as 1 electron volt or 1eV, i.e., 1 eV=1.6 × 10–19J.

tex.back:
Thus, if an electron with charge $q = e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$ is accelerated by a potential difference of $\Delta V = 1$ volt, it would gain energy of $q\Delta V = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$.
This unit of energy is defined as 1 electron volt or 1eV, i.e., $1\ \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$.

source.section: Potential energy of a single charge

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: potential energy of two charges q1 and q2 at r1 and r2 in an external potential V(r).
cards.back:
Potential energy of the system
= the total work done in assembling the configuration
= q1V (r1 ) + q2V (r2 ) + q1q2 4πε0r12
cards.quote: Potential energy of the system = the total work done in assembling the configuration = q1V (r1 ) + q2V (r2 ) + q1q2 4πε0r12

tex.back:
Potential energy of the system
= the total work done in assembling the configuration
$$= q_1 V(\mathbf{r}_1) + q_2 V(\mathbf{r}_2) + \frac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_{12}}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does a dipole experience in a uniform electric field?
cards.back: in a uniform electric field, the dipole experiences no net force; but experiences a torque
cards.quote: in a uniform electric field, the dipole experiences no net force; but experiences a torque

source.section: Potential Energy of a Dipole in an External Field

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: torque τ on a dipole of moment p placed in a uniform electric field E.
cards.back:
As seen in the last chapter, in a uniform electric field, the dipole experiences no net force; but experiences a torque t given by
t=p × E
which will tend to rotate it (unless p is parallel or antiparallel to E).
cards.quote: As seen in the last chapter, in a uniform electric field, the dipole experiences no net force; but experiences a torque t given by t=p × E (2.30) which will tend to rotate it (unless p is parallel or antiparallel to E).

tex.back:
As seen in the last chapter, in a uniform electric field, the dipole experiences no net force; but experiences a torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ given by
$$\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{E}$$
which will tend to rotate it (unless $\mathbf{p}$ is parallel or antiparallel to $\mathbf{E}$).

source.section: Potential energy of a dipole in an external field

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: work W done by the external torque in rotating a dipole of moment p from angle θ0 to θ1 in a uniform field E.
cards.back: W = pE (cosθ0 − cosθ1 )
cards.quote: W = pE (cosθ0 − cosθ1 )

tex.back: $$W = pE(\cos\theta_0 - \cos\theta_1)$$

source.section: Potential energy of a dipole in an external field

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: potential energy of a dipole moment p in a uniform electric field E.
cards.back: The potential energy of a dipole moment p in a uniform electric field E is −p.E.
cards.quote: The potential energy of a dipole moment p in a uniform electric field E is −p.E.

source.section: Potential Energy of a Dipole in an External Field

cards.note: p and E are vectors; p.E is their dot product (scalar product).

tex.back: The potential energy of a dipole moment $\mathbf{p}$ in a uniform electric field $\mathbf{E}$ is $-\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{E}$.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Charged spherical shell: is the electric potential continuous across the surface, and what is its value at the surface?
cards.back: Electric potential is, however continuous across the surface, equal to q/4pe 0R at the surface.
cards.quote: Electric potential is, however continuous across the surface, equal to q/4pe 0R at the surface.

tex.back: Electric potential is, however continuous across the surface, equal to $q/4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$ at the surface.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When does a dipole in a uniform field eventually align with the field?
cards.back: Only if there is a dissipative mechanism, the oscillations are damped and the dipole eventually aligns with E.
cards.quote: Only if there is a dissipative mechanism, the oscillations are damped and the dipole eventually aligns with E.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the potential due to a charge q at its own location?
cards.back: Potential due to a charge q at its own location is not defined – it is infinite.
cards.quote: Potential due to a charge q at its own location is not defined – it is infinite.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What do conductors contain, and what are the charge carriers in metallic conductors?
cards.back: Conductors contain mobile charge carriers. In metallic conductors, these charge carriers are electrons.
cards.quote: Conductors contain mobile charge carriers. In metallic conductors, these charge carriers are electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which electrons are free to move in a metal?
cards.back: In a metal, the outer (valence) electrons part away from their atoms and are free to move.
cards.quote: In a metal, the outer (valence) electrons part away from their atoms and are free to move.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the static situation, what is the electric field inside a conductor?
cards.back: In the static situation, when there is no current inside or on the surface of the conductor, the electric field is zero everywhere inside the conductor.
cards.quote: In the static situation, when there is no current inside or on the surface of the conductor, the electric field is zero everywhere inside the conductor.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is the electrostatic field directed at the surface of a charged conductor?
cards.back: Thus electrostatic field at the surface of a charged conductor must be normal to the surface at every point.
cards.quote: Thus electrostatic field at the surface of a charged conductor must be normal to the surface at every point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where can the excess charge on a charged conductor reside in the static situation?
cards.back: When the conductor is charged, the excess charge can reside only on the surface in the static situation.
cards.quote: When the conductor is charged, the excess charge can reside only on the surface in the static situation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What can be said about the electrostatic potential throughout a conductor and on its surface?
cards.back: Electrostatic potential is constant throughout the volume of the conductor and has the same value (as inside) on its surface
cards.quote: Electrostatic potential is constant throughout the volume of the conductor and has the same value (as inside) on its surface

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a system of conductors, how is the potential of each conductor characterised?
cards.back: In a system of conductors of arbitrary size, shape and charge configuration, each conductor is characterised by a constant value of potential, but this constant may differ from one conductor to the other.
cards.quote: In a system of conductors of arbitrary size, shape and charge configuration, each conductor is characterised by a constant value of potential, but this constant may differ from one conductor to the other.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: electric field E at the surface of a charged conductor with surface charge density σ.
cards.back:
Electric field at the surface of a charged conductor
E = σ nˆ ε0
where s is the surface charge density and nˆ is a unit vector normal to the surface in the outward direction.
cards.quote: Electric field at the surface of a charged conductor E = σ nˆ ε0 (2.35) where s is the surface charge density and nˆ is a unit vector normal to the surface in the outward direction.

tex.back:
Electric field at the surface of a charged conductor
