cards.quote: The ray incident at any angle at the pole. The reflected ray follows laws of reflection.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: the mirror equation relating object distance u, image distance v and focal length f.
cards.back:
Mirror equation:
1+1 = 1 vu f
where u and v are object and image distances, respectively and f is the focal length of the mirror.
cards.quote: Mirror equation: 1+1 = 1 vu f where u and v are object and image distances, respectively and f is the focal length of the mirror.

tex.back:
Mirror equation:
$$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$
where $u$ and $v$ are object and image distances, respectively and $f$ is the focal length of the mirror.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define linear magnification (m) produced by a mirror.
cards.back: We define linear magnification (m) as the ratio of the height of the image (h′) to the height of the object (h)
cards.quote: We define linear magnification (m) as the ratio of the height of the image (h′) to the height of the object (h)
cards.note: For a mirror, m = h'/h = -v/u. Negative m means a real, inverted image.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: linear magnification m of a spherical mirror in terms of image height h′, object height h and distances v, u.
cards.back: m = h′ h = – v u
cards.quote: so that m = h′ h = – v u (9.9)

tex.back: $$m = \frac{h'}{h} = -\frac{v}{u}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For which mirrors and images are the mirror equation and magnification formula valid?
cards.back: With the proper use of sign convention, these are, in fact, valid for all the cases of reflection by a spherical mirror (concave or convex) whether the image formed is real or virtual.
cards.quote: With the proper use of sign convention, these are, in fact, valid for all the cases of reflection by a spherical mirror (concave or convex) whether the image formed is real or virtual.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The lower half of a concave mirror is covered with opaque material. What happens to the image of an object?
cards.back: the image will be that of the whole object. However, as the area of the reflecting surface has been reduced, the intensity of the image will be low (in this case, half).
cards.quote: the image will be that of the whole object. However, as the area of the reflecting surface has been reduced, the intensity of the image will be low (in this case, half).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define refraction of light.
cards.back: The direction of propagation of an obliquely incident (0°< i < 90°) ray of light that enters the other medium, changes at the interface of the two media. This phenomenon is called refraction of light.
cards.quote: The direction of propagation of an obliquely incident (0°< i < 90°) ray of light that enters the other medium, changes at the interface of the two media. This phenomenon is called refraction of light.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Snell's laws of refraction.
cards.back:
The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane.
The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is constant.
cards.quote: (i) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane. (ii) The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is constant.
cards.note: Snell's law: sin i / sin r = n21, the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: Snell's law of refraction, relating sin i, sin r and the refractive index n₂₁.
cards.back:
The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is constant.
Remember that the angles of incidence (i ) and refraction (r ) are the angles that the incident and its refracted ray make with the normal, respectively. We have
sin i sin r = n 21
cards.quote: The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is constant. Remember that the angles of incidence (i ) and refraction (r ) are the angles that the incident and its refracted ray make with the normal, respectively. We have sin i sin r = n 21 (9.10)

tex.back:
The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is constant.
Remember that the angles of incidence ($i$) and refraction ($r$) are the angles that the incident and its refracted ray make with the normal, respectively. We have
$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = n_{21}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For a ray refracting from medium 1 into medium 2, sin i / sin r = n₂₁: what is the constant n₂₁ called?
cards.back:
We have
21 sin sin i n r = (9.10)
where n21 is a constant, called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first medium.
cards.quote: We have 21 sin sin i n r = (9.10) where n21 is a constant, called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first medium.

tex.back:
We have
$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = n_{21} \qquad \text{(9.10)}$$
where $n_{21}$ is a constant, called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first medium.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The refractive index of one medium with respect to another is a characteristic of what, and what does it not depend on?
cards.back: We note that n 21 is a characteristic of the pair of media (and also depends on the wavelength of light), but is independent of the angle of incidence.
cards.quote: We note that n 21 is a characteristic of the pair of media (and also depends on the wavelength of light), but is independent of the angle of incidence.

tex.back: We note that $n_{21}$ is a characteristic of the pair of media (and also depends on the wavelength of light), but is independent of the angle of incidence.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When a refracted ray bends towards the normal, what is the second medium said to be?
cards.back: the refracted ray bends towards the normal. In such a case medium 2 is said to be optically denser (or denser, in short) than medium 1.
cards.quote: the refracted ray bends towards the normal. In such a case medium 2 is said to be optically denser (or denser, in short) than medium 1.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A ray goes from a denser medium into a rarer medium. How does it bend?
cards.back: refracted ray bends away from the normal. This is the case when incident ray in a denser medium refracts into a rarer medium.
cards.quote: refracted ray bends away from the normal. This is the case when incident ray in a denser medium refracts into a rarer medium.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Optical density vs mass density.
cards.back: Optical density should not be confused with mass density, which is mass per unit volume. It is possible that mass density of an optically denser medium may be less than that of an optically rarer medium (optical density is the ratio of the speed of light in two media).
cards.quote: Optical density should not be confused with mass density, which is mass per unit volume. It is possible that mass density of an optically denser medium may be less than that of an optically rarer medium (optical density is the ratio of the speed of light in two media).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Turpentine and water: compare their mass density and their optical density.
cards.back: Mass density of turpentine is less than that of water but its optical density is higher.
cards.quote: Mass density of turpentine is less than that of water but its optical density is higher.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: refractive index n₁₂ of medium 1 with respect to medium 2, in terms of n₂₁.
cards.back:
If n 21 is the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 and n12 the refractive index of medium 1 with respect to medium 2, then it should be clear that
n12 = 1 n 21
cards.quote: If n 21 is the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 and n12 the refractive index of medium 1 with respect to medium 2, then it should be clear that n12 = 1 n 21 (9.11)

tex.back:
If $n_{21}$ is the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 and $n_{12}$ the refractive index of medium 1 with respect to medium 2, then it should be clear that
$$n_{12} = \frac{1}{n_{21}}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: refractive index n₃₂ of medium 3 with respect to medium 2, in terms of n₃₁ and n₁₂.
cards.back: It also follows that if n 32 is the refractive index of medium 3 with respect to medium 2 then n 32 = n 31 × n 12 , where n 31 is the refractive index of medium 3 with respect to medium 1.
cards.quote: It also follows that if n 32 is the refractive index of medium 3 with respect to medium 2 then n 32 = n 31 × n 12 , where n 31 is the refractive index of medium 3 with respect to medium 1.

tex.back: It also follows that if $n_{32}$ is the refractive index of medium 3 with respect to medium 2 then $n_{32} = n_{31} \times n_{12}$, where $n_{31}$ is the refractive index of medium 3 with respect to medium 1.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A ray passes through a rectangular glass slab. Is the emergent ray deviated or shifted?
cards.back: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray—there is no deviation, but it does suffer lateral displacement/shift with respect to the incident ray.
cards.quote: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray—there is no deviation, but it does suffer lateral displacement/shift with respect to the incident ray.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Near-normal viewing of the bottom of a tank of water: how is the apparent depth related to the real depth?
cards.back: For viewing near the normal direction, it can be shown that the apparent depth (h1) is real depth (h2) divided by the refractive index of the medium (water).
cards.quote: For viewing near the normal direction, it can be shown that the apparent depth (h1) is real depth (h2) divided by the refractive index of the medium (water).

tex.back: For viewing near the normal direction, it can be shown that the apparent depth ($h_1$) is real depth ($h_2$) divided by the refractive index of the medium (water).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is internal reflection?
cards.back: When light travels from an optically denser medium to a rarer medium at the interface, it is partly reflected back into the same medium and partly refracted to the second medium. This reflection is called the internal reflection.
cards.quote: When light travels from an optically denser medium to a rarer medium at the interface, it is partly reflected back into the same medium and partly refracted to the second medium. This reflection is called the internal reflection.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In total internal reflection, on the other hand, ____ of light takes place.
cards.back: In total internal reflection, on the other hand, no transmission of light takes place.
cards.quote: In total internal reflection, on the other hand, no transmission of light takes place.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the critical angle of incidence for a ray going from a denser to a rarer medium, and say what occurs for larger angles.
cards.back: The critical angle of incidence ic for a ray incident from a denser to rarer medium, is that angle for which the angle of refraction is 90°. For i > ic, total internal reflection occurs.
cards.quote: The critical angle of incidence ic for a ray incident from a denser to rarer medium, is that angle for which the angle of refraction is 90°. For i > ic, total internal reflection occurs.
cards.note: The critical angle i_c satisfies sin(i_c) = 1/n for a denser medium of refractive index n in air.

tex.back: The critical angle of incidence $i_c$ for a ray incident from a denser to rarer medium, is that angle for which the angle of refraction is $90^\circ$. For $i > i_c$, total internal reflection occurs.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: sine of the critical angle ic for light going into a rarer medium, in terms of the relative refractive index n₂₁.
cards.back:
We see from Snell’s law [Eq. (9.10)] that if the relative refractive index of the refracting medium is less than one then, since the maximum value of sin r is unity, there is an upper limit to the value of sin i for which the law can be satisfied, that is, i = ic such that
sin ic = n 21
cards.quote: We see from Snell’s law [Eq. (9.10)] that if the relative refractive index of the refracting medium is less than one then, since the maximum value of sin r is unity, there is an upper limit to the value of sin i for which the law can be satisfied, that is, i = ic such that sin ic = n 21 (9.12)

tex.back:
We see from Snell’s law [Eq. (9.10)] that if the relative refractive index of the refracting medium is less than one then, since the maximum value of $\sin r$ is unity, there is an upper limit to the value of $\sin i$ for which the law can be satisfied, that is, $i = i_c$ such that
$$\sin i_c = n_{21}$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is total internal reflection used in prisms?
cards.back: Prisms designed to bend light by 90° or by 180° make use of total internal reflection [Fig. 9.13(a) and (b)]. Such a prism is also used to invert images without changing their size [Fig. 9.13(c)].
cards.quote: Prisms designed to bend light by 90° or by 180° make use of total internal reflection [Fig. 9.13(a) and (b)]. Such a prism is also used to invert images without changing their size [Fig. 9.13(c)].

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is an optical fibre made of, and how do the refractive indices of its parts compare?
cards.back: Each fibre consists of a core and cladding. The refractive index of the material of the core is higher than that of the cladding.
cards.quote: Each fibre consists of a core and cladding. The refractive index of the material of the core is higher than that of the cladding.

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does a light signal travel along an optical fibre?
cards.back: When a signal in the form of light is directed at one end of the fibre at a suitable angle, it undergoes repeated total internal reflections along the length of the fibre and finally comes out at the other end (Fig. 9.14).
cards.quote: When a signal in the form of light is directed at one end of the fibre at a suitable angle, it undergoes repeated total internal reflections along the length of the fibre and finally comes out at the other end (Fig. 9.14).

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Since light undergoes total internal reflection at each stage, there is ____ in the intensity of the light signal.
cards.back: Since light undergoes total internal reflection at each stage, there is no appreciable loss in the intensity of the light signal.
cards.quote: Since light undergoes total internal reflection at each stage, there is no appreciable loss in the intensity of the light signal.

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why can an optical fibre act as an optical pipe even when it is bent?
cards.back: Optical fibres are fabricated such that light reflected at one side of inner surface strikes the other at an angle larger than the critical angle. Even if the fibre is bent, light can easily travel along its length. Thus, an optical fibre can be used to act as an optical pipe.
cards.quote: Optical fibres are fabricated such that light reflected at one side of inner surface strikes the other at an angle larger than the critical angle. Even if the fibre is bent, light can easily travel along its length. Thus, an optical fibre can be used to act as an optical pipe.

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Give a medical use of optical fibres as a 'light pipe'.
cards.back: For example, these are used as a ‘light pipe’ to facilitate visual examination of internal organs like esophagus, stomach and intestines.
cards.quote: For example, these are used as a ‘light pipe’ to facilitate visual examination of internal organs like esophagus, stomach and intestines.

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the main requirement in fabricating optical fibres?
cards.back: The main requirement in fabricating optical fibres is that there should be very little absorption of light as it travels for long distances inside them.
cards.quote: The main requirement in fabricating optical fibres is that there should be very little absorption of light as it travels for long distances inside them.

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Optical fibres: what coats the glass fibre, and what happens to light even if the fibre is bent?
cards.back: Optical fibres consist of glass fibres coated with a thin layer of material of lower refractive index. Light incident at an angle at one end comes out at the other, after multiple internal reflections, even if the fibre is bent.
cards.quote: Optical fibres consist of glass fibres coated with a thin layer of material of lower refractive index. Light incident at an angle at one end comes out at the other, after multiple internal reflections, even if the fibre is bent.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a thin lens?
cards.back: A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical.
cards.quote: A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical.

source.section: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the focus and the focal length of a lens.
cards.back: The point where image of an object placed at infinity is formed is called the focus F, of the lens and the distance f gives its focal length.
cards.quote: The point where image of an object placed at infinity is formed is called the focus F, of the lens and the distance f gives its focal length.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How many foci does a lens have?
cards.back: A lens has two foci, F and F′, on either side of it (Fig. 9.17).
cards.quote: A lens has two foci, F and F′, on either side of it (Fig. 9.17).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the lens maker's formula useful for?
cards.back: It is useful to design lenses of desired focal length using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature.
cards.quote: It is useful to design lenses of desired focal length using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature.
cards.note: Lens maker's formula: 1/f = [(n2 - n1)/n1] x (1/R1 - 1/R2); n2 = lens material, n1 = surrounding medium.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Lens maker's formula for a concave lens: what are the signs of R₁, R₂ and f?
cards.back: Note that the formula is true for a concave lens also. In that case R1 is negative, R2 positive and therefore, f is negative.
cards.quote: Note that the formula is true for a concave lens also. In that case R1 is negative, R2 positive and therefore, f is negative.

tex.back: Note that the formula is true for a concave lens also. In that case $R_1$ is negative, $R_2$ positive and therefore, $f$ is negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Sign of the focal length f of a converging lens and of a diverging lens.
cards.back: f is positive for a converging lens; f is negative for a diverging lens.
cards.quote: f is positive for a converging lens; f is negative for a diverging lens.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: the thin lens formula relating object distance u, image distance v and focal length f.
cards.back:
1−1=1 vu f
Equation (9.23) is the familiar thin lens formula.
cards.quote: BO = – u, DI = +v, we get 1−1=1 vu f (9.23) Equation (9.23) is the familiar thin lens formula.

tex.back:
$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$
Equation (9.23) is the familiar thin lens formula.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For which lenses and images is the thin lens formula valid?
cards.back: Equation (9.23) is the familiar thin lens formula. Though we derived it for a real image formed by a convex lens, the formula is valid for both convex as well as concave lenses and for both real and virtual images.
cards.quote: Equation (9.23) is the familiar thin lens formula. Though we derived it for a real image formed by a convex lens, the formula is valid for both convex as well as concave lenses and for both real and virtual images.
cards.note: Thin lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f (Cartesian sign convention).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where are the two foci of a double convex or concave lens, and what are they called?
cards.back: the two foci, F and F′, of a double convex or concave lens are equidistant from the optical centre. The focus on the side of the (original) source of light is called the first focal point, whereas the other is called the second focal point.
cards.quote: the two foci, F and F′, of a double convex or concave lens are equidistant from the optical centre. The focus on the side of the (original) source of light is called the first focal point, whereas the other is called the second focal point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Rays used to locate an image formed by a lens.
cards.back:
A ray emanating from the object parallel to the principal axis of the lens after refraction passes through the second principal focus F′ (in a convex lens) or appears to diverge (in a concave lens) from the first principal focus F.
A ray of light, passing through the optical centre of the lens, emerges without any deviation after refraction.
A ray of light passing through the first principal focus of a convex lens [Fig. 9.17(a)] emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction.
A ray of light incident on a concave lens appearing to meet the principal axis at second focus point emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction [Fig. 9.17(b)].
cards.quote: (i) A ray emanating from the object parallel to the principal axis of the lens after refraction passes through the second principal focus F′ (in a convex lens) or appears to diverge (in a concave lens) from the first principal focus F. (ii) A ray of light, passing through the optical centre of the lens, emerges without any deviation after refraction. (iii) (a) A ray of light passing through the first principal focus of a convex lens [Fig. 9.17(a)] emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction. (b) A ray of light incident on a concave lens appearing to meet the principal axis at second focus point emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction [Fig. 9.17(b)].

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Lens ray diagram: what happens to a ray passing through the optical centre?
cards.back: A ray of light, passing through the optical centre of the lens, emerges without any deviation after refraction.
cards.quote: A ray of light, passing through the optical centre of the lens, emerges without any deviation after refraction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the magnification (m) produced by a lens.
cards.back: Magnification (m) produced by a lens is defined, like that for a mirror, as the ratio of the size of the image to that of the object.
cards.quote: Magnification (m) produced by a lens is defined, like that for a mirror, as the ratio of the size of the image to that of the object.
cards.note: For a lens, m = h'/h = v/u.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Sign of the magnification m for an erect (virtual) image and for an inverted (real) image formed by a lens.
cards.back: When we apply the sign convention, we see that, for erect (and virtual) image formed by a convex or concave lens, m is positive, while for an inverted (and real) image, m is negative.
cards.quote: When we apply the sign convention, we see that, for erect (and virtual) image formed by a convex or concave lens, m is positive, while for an inverted (and real) image, m is negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A glass lens of refractive index 1.47 disappears in a liquid. What is the refractive index of the liquid?
cards.back: The refractive index of the liquid must be equal to 1.47 in order to make the lens disappear.
cards.quote: The refractive index of the liquid must be equal to 1.47 in order to make the lens disappear.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does the power of a lens measure?
cards.back: Power of a lens is a measure of the convergence or divergence, which a lens introduces in the light falling on it.
cards.quote: Power of a lens is a measure of the convergence or divergence, which a lens introduces in the light falling on it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the power P of a lens.
cards.back: The power P of a lens is defined as the tangent of the angle by which it converges or diverges a beam of light parallel to the principal axis falling at unit distance from the optical centre (Fig. 9.18).
cards.quote: The power P of a lens is defined as the tangent of the angle by which it converges or diverges a beam of light parallel to the principal axis falling at unit distance from the optical centre (Fig. 9.18).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: power P of a lens in terms of its focal length f.
cards.back: The power of a lens P = 1/f.
cards.quote: The power of a lens P = 1/f.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of the power of a lens?
cards.back: The SI unit for power of a lens is dioptre (D)
cards.quote: The SI unit for power of a lens is dioptre (D)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The power of a lens of focal length of 1 metre is ____.
cards.back: The power of a lens of focal length of 1 metre is one dioptre.
cards.quote: The power of a lens of focal length of 1 metre is one dioptre.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Sign of the power of a converging lens and of a diverging lens.
cards.back: Power of a lens is positive for a converging lens and negative for a diverging lens.
cards.quote: Power of a lens is positive for a converging lens and negative for a diverging lens.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What lens does a power of +2.5 D mean, and what lens does -4.0 D mean?
cards.back: Thus, when an optician prescribes a corrective lens of power + 2.5 D, the required lens is a convex lens of focal length + 40 cm. A lens of power of – 4.0 D means a concave lens of focal length – 25 cm.
cards.quote: Thus, when an optician prescribes a corrective lens of power + 2.5 D, the required lens is a convex lens of focal length + 40 cm. A lens of power of – 4.0 D means a concave lens of focal length – 25 cm.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: effective focal length f of thin lenses of focal lengths f₁, f₂, f₃,… in contact.
cards.back:
If several thin lenses of focal length f1, f2, f3,... are in contact, the effective focal length of their combination is given by
1= 1 + 1 + 1 +… f f1 f2 f3
cards.quote: If several thin lenses of focal length f1, f2, f3,... are in contact, the effective focal length of their combination is given by 1= 1 + 1 + 1 +… f f1 f2 f3

source.section: Combination of thin lenses in contact

tex.back:
If several thin lenses of focal length $f_1, f_2, f_3, \ldots$ are in contact, the effective focal length of their combination is given by
$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} + \frac{1}{f_3} + \ldots$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Lenses in contact: how are the individual powers added, convex and concave lenses together?
cards.back: Note that the sum in Eq. (9.32) is an algebraic sum of individual powers, so some of the terms on the right side may be positive (for convex lenses) and some negative (for concave lenses).
cards.quote: Note that the sum in Eq. (9.32) is an algebraic sum of individual powers, so some of the terms on the right side may be positive (for convex lenses) and some negative (for concave lenses).

source.section: Combination of thin lenses in contact

cards.note: For thin lenses in contact the net power is the sum of the individual powers, and the net 1/f is the sum of the individual 1/f values.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For a combination of thin lenses in contact, how is the total magnification m related to m1, m2, m3 of the individual lenses?
cards.back:
A product.
the total magnification m of the combination is a product of magnification (m1, m2, m3,...) of individual lenses
cards.quote: the total magnification m of the combination is a product of magnification (m1, m2, m3,...) of individual lenses

source.section: Combination of thin lenses in contact

cards.note: In symbols: m = m1 x m2 x m3 x ... (the product of the individual magnifications, not the sum).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What do combinations of lenses help to obtain, and what do they enhance?
cards.back: Combination of lenses helps to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired magnification. It also enhances sharpness of the image.
cards.quote: Combination of lenses helps to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired magnification. It also enhances sharpness of the image.

source.section: Combination of thin lenses in contact

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where is a combination of lenses commonly used?
cards.back: Such a system of combination of lenses is commonly used in designing lenses for cameras, microscopes, telescopes and other optical instruments.
cards.quote: Such a system of combination of lenses is commonly used in designing lenses for cameras, microscopes, telescopes and other optical instruments.

source.section: Combination of thin lenses in contact

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the angle of deviation for a ray passing through a prism (incident ray PQ, emergent ray RS).
cards.back: The angle between the emergent ray RS and the direction of the incident ray PQ is called the angle of deviation
cards.quote: The angle between the emergent ray RS and the direction of the incident ray PQ is called the angle of deviation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: for a prism of angle A, with r₁ the refraction angle at the first face and r₂ the incidence angle at the second, find r₁ + r₂.
cards.back: r1 + r2 = A
cards.quote: Comparing these two equations, we get r1 + r2 = A (9.34)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: angle of deviation δ of a ray through a prism of angle A, in terms of i and the angle of emergence e.
cards.back:
The total deviation d is the sum of deviations at the two faces,
d = (i – r1 ) + (e – r2 )
that is,
d =i+e–A
cards.quote: The total deviation d is the sum of deviations at the two faces, d = (i – r1 ) + (e – r2 ) that is, d =i+e–A (9.35)

tex.back:
The total deviation $\delta$ is the sum of deviations at the two faces,
$$\delta = (i - r_1) + (e - r_2)$$
that is,
$$\delta = i + e - A$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: At the minimum deviation Dₘ of a prism, how does the refracted ray lie inside the prism relative to its base?
cards.back: At the minimum deviation Dm, the refracted ray inside the prism becomes parallel to its base.
cards.quote: At the minimum deviation Dm, the refracted ray inside the prism becomes parallel to its base.

tex.back: At the minimum deviation $D_m$, the refracted ray inside the prism becomes parallel to its base.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: refractive index n₂₁ of a prism material in terms of the prism angle A and the angle of minimum deviation Dₘ.
cards.back:
For a prism of the angle A, of refractive index n 2 placed in a medium of refractive index n 1,
n 21 = n2 n1 = sin (A + D m )/2 sin (A / 2)
where D m is the angle of minimum deviation.
cards.quote: For a prism of the angle A, of refractive index n 2 placed in a medium of refractive index n 1, n 21 = n2 n1 = sin (A + D m )/2 sin (A / 2) where D m is the angle of minimum deviation.

tex.back:
For a prism of the angle $A$, of refractive index $n_2$ placed in a medium of refractive index $n_1$,
$$n_{21} = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{\sin\left[(A + D_m)/2\right]}{\sin(A/2)}$$
where $D_m$ is the angle of minimum deviation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: angle of minimum deviation Dₘ of a thin prism of angle A and relative refractive index n₂₁.
cards.back:
Dm = (n21–1)A
It implies that, thin prisms do not deviate light much.
cards.quote: Dm = (n21–1)A It implies that, thin prisms do not deviate light much.

tex.back:
$$D_m = (n_{21} - 1)A$$
It implies that, thin prisms do not deviate light much.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define dispersion of light.
cards.back: Dispersion is the splitting of light into its constituent colour.
cards.quote: Dispersion is the splitting of light into its constituent colour.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why do thick lenses give coloured images?
cards.back: Thick lenses give coloured images due to dispersion.
cards.quote: Thick lenses give coloured images due to dispersion.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a simple magnifier or microscope?
cards.back: A simple magnifier or microscope is a converging lens of small focal length (Fig. 9.23).
cards.quote: A simple magnifier or microscope is a converging lens of small focal length (Fig. 9.23).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is a converging lens used as a simple microscope?
cards.back: In order to use such a lens as a microscope, the lens is held near the object, one focal length away or less, and the eye is positioned close to the lens on the other side.
cards.quote: In order to use such a lens as a microscope, the lens is held near the object, one focal length away or less, and the eye is positioned close to the lens on the other side.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What image does a simple microscope aim to give?
cards.back: The idea is to get an erect, magnified and virtual image of the object at a distance so that it can be viewed comfortably, i.e., at 25 cm or more.
cards.quote: The idea is to get an erect, magnified and virtual image of the object at a distance so that it can be viewed comfortably, i.e., at 25 cm or more.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Simple microscope: where is the image if the object is at a distance f?
cards.back: If the object is at a distance f, the image is at infinity.
cards.quote: If the object is at a distance f, the image is at infinity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where is the image formed by a simple microscope often considered most suitable for viewing by the relaxed eye?
cards.back:
At infinity.
Therefore, the image formed at infinity is often considered most suitable for viewing by the relaxed eye.
cards.quote: Therefore, the image formed at infinity is often considered most suitable for viewing by the relaxed eye.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnifying power m of a simple microscope.
cards.back: Magnifying power m of a simple microscope is given by m = 1 + (D/f), where D = 25 cm is the least distance of distinct vision and f is the focal length of the convex lens.
cards.quote: Magnifying power m of a simple microscope is given by m = 1 + (D/f), where D = 25 cm is the least distance of distinct vision and f is the focal length of the convex lens.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnifying power of a simple microscope when the image is at infinity.
cards.back: If the image is at infinity, m = D/f.
cards.quote: If the image is at infinity, m = D/f.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does a single-lens simple magnifier allow you to do with the object, compared with the near point D?
cards.back: What a single-lens simple magnifier achieves is that it allows the object to be brought closer to the eye than D.
cards.quote: What a single-lens simple magnifier achieves is that it allows the object to be brought closer to the eye than D.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a compound microscope?
cards.back: For much larger magnifications, one uses two lenses, one compounding the effect of the other. This is known as a compound microscope.
cards.quote: For much larger magnifications, one uses two lenses, one compounding the effect of the other. This is known as a compound microscope.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Compound microscope: what do the objective and the eyepiece each do?
cards.back: The lens nearest the object, called the objective, forms a real, inverted, magnified image of the object. This serves as the object for the second lens, the eyepiece, which functions essentially like a simple microscope or magnifier, produces the final image, which is enlarged and virtual.
cards.quote: The lens nearest the object, called the objective, forms a real, inverted, magnified image of the object. This serves as the object for the second lens, the eyepiece, which functions essentially like a simple microscope or magnifier, produces the final image, which is enlarged and virtual.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Clearly, the final image is ____ with respect to the original object.
cards.back: Clearly, the final image is inverted with respect to the original object.
cards.quote: Clearly, the final image is inverted with respect to the original object.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the tube length of a compound microscope.
cards.back: The distance L, i.e., the distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece (focal length fe) is called the tube length of the compound microscope.
cards.quote: The distance L, i.e., the distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece (focal length fe) is called the tube length of the compound microscope.

tex.back: The distance $L$, i.e., the distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece (focal length $f_e$) is called the tube length of the compound microscope.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnifying power m of a compound microscope (D = 25 cm, least distance of distinct vision) in terms of mₑ, mₒ, L, fₒ, fₑ.
cards.back:
For a compound microscope, the magnifying power is given by
m = me × m0
where me = 1 + (D/fe), is the magnification due to the eyepiece and mo is the magnification produced by the objective.
Approximately,
m= L ×D fo fe
where fo and fe are the focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece, respectively, and L is the distance between their focal points.
cards.quote: For a compound microscope, the magnifying power is given by m = me × m0 where me = 1 + (D/fe), is the magnification due to the eyepiece and mo is the magnification produced by the objective. Approximately, m= L ×D fo fe where fo and fe are the focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece, respectively, and L is the distance between their focal points.

tex.back:
For a compound microscope, the magnifying power is given by
$$m = m_e \times m_0$$
where $m_e = 1 + (D/f_e)$, is the magnification due to the eyepiece and $m_o$ is the magnification produced by the objective.
Approximately,
$$m = \frac{L}{f_o} \times \frac{D}{f_e}$$
where $f_o$ and $f_e$ are the focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece, respectively, and $L$ is the distance between their focal points.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For large magnification, what should be true of the focal lengths of a compound microscope's objective and eyepiece?
cards.back: Clearly, to achieve a large magnification of a small object (hence the name microscope), the objective and eyepiece should have small focal lengths.
cards.quote: Clearly, to achieve a large magnification of a small object (hence the name microscope), the objective and eyepiece should have small focal lengths.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why are multicomponent lenses used in modern microscopes?
cards.back: In modern microscopes, multicomponent lenses are used for both the objective and the eyepiece to improve image quality by minimising various optical aberrations (defects) in lenses.
cards.quote: In modern microscopes, multicomponent lenses are used for both the objective and the eyepiece to improve image quality by minimising various optical aberrations (defects) in lenses.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the telescope used for?
cards.back: The telescope is used to provide angular magnification of distant objects (Fig. 9.25).
cards.quote: The telescope is used to provide angular magnification of distant objects (Fig. 9.25).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Telescope: how does the objective compare with the eyepiece?
cards.back: It also has an objective and an eyepiece. But here, the objective has a large focal length and a much larger aperture than the eyepiece.
cards.quote: It also has an objective and an eyepiece. But here, the objective has a large focal length and a much larger aperture than the eyepiece.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Refracting telescope: how is the final image formed?
cards.back: Light from a distant object enters the objective and a real image is formed in the tube at its second focal point. The eyepiece magnifies this image producing a final inverted image.
cards.quote: Light from a distant object enters the objective and a real image is formed in the tube at its second focal point. The eyepiece magnifies this image producing a final inverted image.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the magnifying power m of a telescope.
cards.back: The magnifying power m is the ratio of the angle b subtended at the eye by the final image to the angle a which the object subtends at the lens or the eye.
cards.quote: The magnifying power m is the ratio of the angle b subtended at the eye by the final image to the angle a which the object subtends at the lens or the eye.
cards.note: Magnifying power of a telescope: m = fo/fe (objective focal length over eyepiece focal length).

tex.back: The magnifying power $m$ is the ratio of the angle $\beta$ subtended at the eye by the final image to the angle $\alpha$ which the object subtends at the lens or the eye.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnifying power m of a telescope as the ratio of the angles β and α, in terms of the focal lengths fₒ and fₑ.
cards.back:
m = β = fo α fe
where f0 and fe are the focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece, respectively.
cards.quote: Magnifying power m of a telescope is the ratio of the angle b subtended at the eye by the image to the angle a subtended at the eye by the object. m = β = fo α fe where f0 and fe are the focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece, respectively.

tex.back:
$$m = \frac{\beta}{\alpha} = \frac{f_o}{f_e}$$
where $f_0$ and $f_e$ are the focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece, respectively.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A telescope has magnifying power m = fₒ/fₑ (focal lengths of objective and eyepiece). What is the length of its tube?
cards.back: In this case, the length of the telescope tube is fo + fe.
cards.quote: In this case, the length of the telescope tube is fo + fe.

tex.back: In this case, the length of the telescope tube is $f_o + f_e$.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How do terrestrial telescopes make the final image erect?
cards.back: Terrestrial telescopes have, in addition, a pair of inverting lenses to make the final image erect.
cards.quote: Terrestrial telescopes have, in addition, a pair of inverting lenses to make the final image erect.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the main considerations with an astronomical telescope?
cards.back: The main considerations with an astronomical telescope are its light gathering power and its resolution or resolving power.
cards.quote: The main considerations with an astronomical telescope are its light gathering power and its resolution or resolving power.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On what does the resolving power of a telescope depend?
cards.back: The resolving power, or the ability to observe two objects distinctly, which are in very nearly the same direction, also depends on the diameter of the objective.
cards.quote: The resolving power, or the ability to observe two objects distinctly, which are in very nearly the same direction, also depends on the diameter of the objective.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the desirable aim in making optical telescopes?
cards.back: So, the desirable aim in optical telescopes is to make them with objective of large diameter.
cards.quote: So, the desirable aim in optical telescopes is to make them with objective of large diameter.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why are very large lens objectives hard to use?
cards.back: Such big lenses tend to be very heavy and therefore, difficult to make and support by their edges.
cards.quote: Such big lenses tend to be very heavy and therefore, difficult to make and support by their edges.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a reflecting telescope, and why does it have no chromatic aberration?
cards.back: For these reasons, modern telescopes use a concave mirror rather than a lens for the objective. Telescopes with mirror objectives are called reflecting telescopes. There is no chromatic aberration in a mirror.
cards.quote: For these reasons, modern telescopes use a concave mirror rather than a lens for the objective. Telescopes with mirror objectives are called reflecting telescopes. There is no chromatic aberration in a mirror.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is mechanical support less of a problem for a mirror objective?
cards.back: Mechanical support is much less of a problem since a mirror weighs much less than a lens of equivalent optical quality, and can be supported over its entire back surface, not just over its rim.
cards.quote: Mechanical support is much less of a problem since a mirror weighs much less than a lens of equivalent optical quality, and can be supported over its entire back surface, not just over its rim.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a Cassegrain telescope, and what is its advantage?
cards.back: One such arrangement using a convex secondary mirror to focus the incident light, which now passes through a hole in the objective primary mirror, is shown in Fig. 9.26. This is known as a Cassegrain telescope, after its inventor. It has the advantages of a large focal length in a short telescope.
cards.quote: One such arrangement using a convex secondary mirror to focus the incident light, which now passes through a hole in the objective primary mirror, is shown in Fig. 9.26. This is known as a Cassegrain telescope, after its inventor. It has the advantages of a large focal length in a short telescope.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where is the largest telescope in India, and what kind is it?
cards.back: The largest telescope in India is in Kavalur, Tamil Nadu. It is a 2.34 m diameter reflecting telescope (Cassegrain).
cards.quote: The largest telescope in India is in Kavalur, Tamil Nadu. It is a 2.34 m diameter reflecting telescope (Cassegrain).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State the Cartesian sign convention.
cards.back:
Distances measured in the same direction as the incident light are positive; those measured in the opposite direction are negative.
All distances are measured from the pole/optic centre of the mirror/lens on the principal axis.
The heights measured upwards above x-axis and normal to the principal axis of the mirror/ lens are taken as positive.
The heights measured downwards are taken as negative.
cards.quote: Distances measured in the same direction as the incident light are positive; those measured in the opposite direction are negative. All distances are measured from the pole/optic centre of the mirror/lens on the principal axis. The heights measured upwards above x-axis and normal to the principal axis of the mirror/ lens are taken as positive. The heights measured downwards are taken as negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Sign of the focal length of a concave mirror and of a convex mirror.
cards.back: f is negative for concave mirror; f is positive for a convex mirror.
cards.quote: f is negative for concave mirror; f is positive for a convex mirror.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The laws of reflection and refraction are true for ____ and pairs of media at the point of the incidence.
cards.back: The laws of reflection and refraction are true for all surfaces and pairs of media at the point of the incidence.
cards.quote: The laws of reflection and refraction are true for all surfaces and pairs of media at the point of the incidence.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why do you not see your image in the page of a book?
cards.back: In principle, all rays from a given point should reach the same image point. This is why you do not see your image by an irregular reflecting object, say the page of a book.
cards.quote: In principle, all rays from a given point should reach the same image point. This is why you do not see your image by an irregular reflecting object, say the page of a book.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: resistivity ρ in terms of electrical conductivity σ
cards.back: electrical conductivity (s ) or resistivity (r = 1/s )
cards.quote: On the basis of the relative values of electrical conductivity (s ) or resistivity (r = 1/s ), the solids are broadly classified as:

tex.back: electrical conductivity ($\sigma$) or resistivity ($\rho = 1/\sigma$)

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does NCERT describe the resistivity of metals?
cards.back: Metals: They possess very low resistivity (or high conductivity).
cards.quote: Metals: They possess very low resistivity (or high conductivity).

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does NCERT describe the resistivity of semiconductors?
cards.back: Semiconductors: They have resistivity or conductivity intermediate to metals and insulators.
cards.quote: Semiconductors: They have resistivity or conductivity intermediate to metals and insulators.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does NCERT describe the resistivity of insulators?
cards.back: Insulators: They have high resistivity (or low conductivity).
cards.quote: Insulators: They have high resistivity (or low conductivity).

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: List the resistivity ρ and conductivity σ ranges NCERT gives for metals, semiconductors and insulators.
cards.back:
Metals: They possess very low resistivity (or high conductivity).
r ~ 10–2 – 10–8 W m
s ~ 102 – 108 S m–1
Semiconductors: They have resistivity or conductivity intermediate to metals and insulators.
r ~ 10–5 – 106 W m
s ~ 105 – 10–6 S m–1
Insulators: They have high resistivity (or low conductivity).
r ~ 1011 – 1019 W m
s ~ 10–11 – 10–19 S m–1
cards.quote: Metals: They possess very low resistivity (or high conductivity). r ~ 10–2 – 10–8 W m s ~ 102 – 108 S m–1 (ii) Semiconductors: They have resistivity or conductivity intermediate to metals and insulators. r ~ 10–5 – 106 W m s ~ 105 – 10–6 S m–1 (iii)Insulators: They have high resistivity (or low conductivity). r ~ 1011 – 1019 W m s ~ 10–11 – 10–19 S m–1

tex.back:
Metals: They possess very low resistivity (or high conductivity).
$\rho \sim 10^{-2}\ \text{–}\ 10^{-8}\ \Omega\ \text{m}$
$\sigma \sim 10^{2}\ \text{–}\ 10^{8}\ \text{S m}^{-1}$
Semiconductors: They have resistivity or conductivity intermediate to metals and insulators.
$\rho \sim 10^{-5}\ \text{–}\ 10^{6}\ \Omega\ \text{m}$
$\sigma \sim 10^{5}\ \text{–}\ 10^{-6}\ \text{S m}^{-1}$
Insulators: They have high resistivity (or low conductivity).
$\rho \sim 10^{11}\ \text{–}\ 10^{19}\ \Omega\ \text{m}$
$\sigma \sim 10^{-11}\ \text{–}\ 10^{-19}\ \text{S m}^{-1}$

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Types of semiconductors (elemental and compound).
cards.back:
Elemental semiconductors: Si and Ge
Compound semiconductors
Inorganic: CdS, GaAs, CdSe, InP, etc.
Organic: anthracene, doped pthalocyanines, etc.
Organic polymers: polypyrrole, polyaniline, polythiophene, etc.
cards.quote: (i) Elemental semiconductors: Si and Ge (ii) Compound semiconductors: Examples are: Inorganic: CdS, GaAs, CdSe, InP, etc. Organic: anthracene, doped pthalocyanines, etc. Organic polymers: polypyrrole, polyaniline, polythiophene, etc.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Most of the currently available semiconductor devices are based on elemental semiconductors ____ and compound inorganic semiconductors.
cards.back: Most of the currently available semiconductor devices are based on elemental semiconductors Si or Ge and compound inorganic semiconductors.
cards.quote: Most of the currently available semiconductor devices are based on elemental semiconductors Si or Ge and compound inorganic semiconductors.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: According to the Bohr atomic model, in an isolated atom the energy of any of its electrons is decided by the ____ in which it revolves.
cards.back: According to the Bohr atomic model, in an isolated atom the energy of any of its electrons is decided by the orbit in which it revolves.
cards.quote: According to the Bohr atomic model, in an isolated atom the energy of any of its electrons is decided by the orbit in which it revolves.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are energy bands?
cards.back: These different energy levels with continuous energy variation form what are called energy bands.
cards.quote: These different energy levels with continuous energy variation form what are called energy bands.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the valence band.
cards.back: The energy band which includes the energy levels of the valence electrons is called the valence band.
cards.quote: The energy band which includes the energy levels of the valence electrons is called the valence band.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the conduction band.
cards.back: The energy band above the valence band is called the conduction band.
cards.quote: The energy band above the valence band is called the conduction band.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: With no external energy, all the valence electrons will reside in the ____.
cards.back: With no external energy, all the valence electrons will reside in the valence band.
cards.quote: With no external energy, all the valence electrons will reside in the valence band.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A Si or Ge crystal has N atoms and so 4N valence electrons: how many energy states are available to them?
cards.back: So, for the 4N valence electrons there are 8N available energy states.
cards.quote: So, for the 4N valence electrons there are 8N available energy states.

tex.back: So, for the $4N$ valence electrons there are $8N$ available energy states.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What do the symbols EC and EV stand for in an energy-band diagram?
cards.back: The lowest energy level in the conduction band is shown as EC and highest energy level in the valence band is shown as EV.
cards.quote: The lowest energy level in the conduction band is shown as EC and highest energy level in the valence band is shown as EV .

tex.back: The lowest energy level in the conduction band is shown as $E_C$ and highest energy level in the valence band is shown as $E_V$.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the energy band gap (energy gap)?
cards.back: The gap between the top of the valence band and bottom of the conduction band is called the energy band gap.
cards.quote: The gap between the top of the valence band and bottom of the conduction band is called the energy band gap.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the energy-band picture, which materials have the conduction band overlapping the valence band?
cards.back: If the lowest level in the conduction band happens to be lower than the highest level of the valence band, the electrons from the valence band can easily move into the conduction band. Normally the conduction band is empty. But when it overlaps on the valence band electrons can move freely into it. This is the case with metallic conductors.
cards.quote: If the lowest level in the conduction band happens to be lower than the highest level of the valence band, the electrons from the valence band can easily move into the conduction band. Normally the conduction band is empty. But when it overlaps on the valence band electrons can move freely into it. This is the case with metallic conductors.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a metal where the bands overlap, what happens to the electrons of the valence band?
cards.back: When there is overlap electrons from valence band can easily move into the conduction band. This situation makes a large number of electrons available for electrical conduction.
cards.quote: When there is overlap electrons from valence band can easily move into the conduction band. This situation makes a large number of electrons available for electrical conduction.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the resistance of materials whose valence band is partially empty (metals)?
cards.back: Therefore, the resistance of such materials is low or the conductivity is high.
cards.quote: Therefore, the resistance of such materials is low or the conductivity is high.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens to the valence electrons if there is a gap between the valence and conduction bands?
cards.back: If there is some gap between the conduction band and the valence band, electrons in the valence band all remain bound and no free electrons are available in the conduction band. This makes the material an insulator.
cards.quote: If there is some gap between the conduction band and the valence band, electrons in the valence band all remain bound and no free electrons are available in the conduction band. This makes the material an insulator.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: There are ____ in the conduction band, and therefore no electrical conduction is possible.
cards.back: There are no electrons in the conduction band, and therefore no electrical conduction is possible.
cards.quote: There are no electrons in the conduction band, and therefore no electrical conduction is possible.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In an insulator, why can electrons not be excited to the conduction band?
cards.back: Note that the energy gap is so large that electrons cannot be excited from the valence band to the conduction band by thermal excitation. This is the case of insulators.
cards.quote: Note that the energy gap is so large that electrons cannot be excited from the valence band to the conduction band by thermal excitation. This is the case of insulators.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why can some electrons of a semiconductor conduct at room temperature?
cards.back: Because of the small band gap, at room temperature some electrons from valence band can acquire enough energy to cross the energy gap and enter the conduction band.
cards.quote: Because of the small band gap, at room temperature some electrons from valence band can acquire enough energy to cross the energy gap and enter the conduction band.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the resistance of semiconductors compare with that of insulators?
cards.back: Hence, the resistance of semiconductors is not as high as that of the insulators.
cards.quote: Hence, the resistance of semiconductors is not as high as that of the insulators.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the energy gaps of C (diamond), Si and Ge?
cards.back: For C (diamond), Si and Ge, the energy gaps are 5.4 eV, 1.1 eV and 0.7 eV, respectively.
cards.quote: For C (diamond), Si and Ge, the energy gaps are 5.4 eV, 1.1 eV and 0.7 eV, respectively.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Sn is a group IV element, so why is it a metal?
cards.back: Sn also is a group IV element but it is a metal because the energy gap in its case is 0 eV.
cards.quote: Sn also is a group IV element but it is a metal because the energy gap in its case is 0 eV.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The difference in the resistivity of C, Si and Ge depends upon the ____ between their conduction and valence bands.
cards.back: The difference in the resistivity of C, Si and Ge depends upon the energy gap between their conduction and valence bands.
cards.quote: The difference in the resistivity of C, Si and Ge depends upon the energy gap between their conduction and valence bands.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a Si or Ge crystal, how does each atom share electrons with its four nearest neighbours?
cards.back: In its crystalline structure, every Si or Ge atom tends to share one of its four valence electrons with each of its four nearest neighbour atoms, and also to take share of one electron from each such neighbour.
cards.quote: In its crystalline structure, every Si or Ge atom tends to share one of its four valence electrons with each of its four nearest neighbour atoms, and also to take share of one electron from each such neighbour.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a covalent bond (valence bond) in Si or Ge?
cards.back: These shared electron pairs are referred to as forming a covalent bond or simply a valence bond.
cards.quote: These shared electron pairs are referred to as forming a covalent bond or simply a valence bond.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the lattice structures of Ge and Si called?
cards.back: We shall take the most common case of Ge and Si whose lattice structure is shown in Fig. 14.3. These structures are called the diamond-like structures.
cards.quote: We shall take the most common case of Ge and Si whose lattice structure is shown in Fig. 14.3. These structures are called the diamond-like structures.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a hole in a semiconductor?
cards.back: This vacancy with the effective positive electronic charge is called a hole. The hole behaves as an apparent free particle with effective positive charge.
cards.quote: This vacancy with the effective positive electronic charge is called a hole. The hole behaves as an apparent free particle with effective positive charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: electron, hole and intrinsic carrier concentrations of an intrinsic semiconductor
cards.back:
In intrinsic semiconductors, the number of free electrons, ne is equal to the number of holes, nh. That is
ne = nh = ni
where ni is called intrinsic carrier concentration.
cards.quote: In intrinsic semiconductors, the number of free electrons, ne is equal to the number of holes, nh . That is ne = nh = ni (14.1) where ni is called intrinsic carrier concentration.

tex.back:
In intrinsic semiconductors, the number of free electrons, $n_e$ is equal to the number of holes, $n_h$. That is
$$n_e = n_h = n_i$$
where $n_i$ is called intrinsic carrier concentration.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are intrinsic semiconductors?
cards.back: Pure semiconductors are called "intrinsic semiconductors". The presence of charge carriers (electrons and holes) is an "intrinsic" property of the material and these are obtained as a result of thermal excitation.
cards.quote: Pure semiconductors are called "intrinsic semiconductors". The presence of charge carriers (electrons and holes) is an "intrinsic" property of the material and these are obtained as a result of thermal excitation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: total current I in a semiconductor in terms of the electron current and the hole current
cards.back:
The total current, I is thus the sum of the electron current Ie and the hole current Ih:
I = Ie + Ih
cards.quote: The total current, I is thus the sum of the electron current Ie and the hole current Ih : I = Ie + Ih (14.2)

tex.back:
The total current, $I$ is thus the sum of the electron current $I_e$ and the hole current $I_h$:
$$I = I_e + I_h$$

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is recombination of charge carriers, and what holds at equilibrium?
cards.back: It may be noted that apart from the process of generation of conduction electrons and holes, a simultaneous process of recombination occurs in which the electrons recombine with the holes. At equilibrium, the rate of generation is equal to the rate of recombination of charge carriers.
cards.quote: It may be noted that apart from the process of generation of conduction electrons and holes, a simultaneous process of recombination occurs in which the electrons recombine with the holes. At equilibrium, the rate of generation is equal to the rate of recombination of charge carriers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An intrinsic semiconductor will behave like an ____ at T = 0 K as shown in Fig. 14.6(a).
cards.back: An intrinsic semiconductor will behave like an insulator at T = 0 K as shown in Fig. 14.6(a).
cards.quote: An intrinsic semiconductor will behave like an insulator at T = 0 K as shown in Fig. 14.6(a).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In an intrinsic semiconductor, what excites some electrons from the valence band to the conduction band at T > 0 K?
cards.back: It is the thermal energy at higher temperatures (T > 0K), which excites some electrons from the valence band to the conduction band.
cards.quote: It is the thermal energy at higher temperatures (T > 0K), which excites some electrons from the valence band to the conduction band.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: ____ and the atomic structure of constituent elements decide whether a particular material will be insulator, metal or semiconductor.
cards.back: Lattice structure and the atomic structure of constituent elements decide whether a particular material will be insulator, metal or semiconductor.
cards.quote: Lattice structure and the atomic structure of constituent elements decide whether a particular material will be insulator, metal or semiconductor.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor depends on its temperature, but at room temperature its conductivity is ____.
cards.back: The conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor depends on its temperature, but at room temperature its conductivity is very low.
cards.quote: The conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor depends on its temperature, but at room temperature its conductivity is very low.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Example 14.1: in which orbits do the 4 bonding electrons of C, Si and Ge lie?
cards.back: The 4 bonding electrons of C, Si or Ge lie, respectively, in the second, third and fourth orbit.
cards.quote: The 4 bonding electrons of C, Si or Ge lie, respectively, in the second, third and fourth orbit.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are extrinsic (impurity) semiconductors?
cards.back: When a small amount, say, a few parts per million (ppm), of a suitable impurity is added to the pure semiconductor, the conductivity of the semiconductor is increased manifold. Such materials are known as extrinsic semiconductors or impurity semiconductors.
cards.quote: When a small amount, say, a few parts per million (ppm), of a suitable impurity is added to the pure semiconductor, the conductivity of the semiconductor is increased manifold. Such materials are known as extrinsic semiconductors or impurity semiconductors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is doping, and what are the impurity atoms called?
cards.back: The deliberate addition of a desirable impurity is called doping and the impurity atoms are called dopants.
cards.quote: The deliberate addition of a desirable impurity is called doping and the impurity atoms are called dopants.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the necessary condition on the size of a dopant atom?
cards.back: A necessary condition to attain this is that the sizes of the dopant and the semiconductor atoms should be nearly the same.
cards.quote: A necessary condition to attain this is that the sizes of the dopant and the semiconductor atoms should be nearly the same.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Types of dopants used in doping tetravalent Si or Ge.
cards.back:
Pentavalent (valency 5); like Arsenic (As), Antimony (Sb), Phosphorous (P), etc.
Trivalent (valency 3); like Indium (In), Boron (B), Aluminium (Al), etc.
cards.quote: There are two types of dopants used in doping the tetravalent Si or Ge: (i) Pentavalent (valency 5); like Arsenic (As), Antimony (Sb), Phosphorous (P), etc. (ii) Trivalent (valency 3); like Indium (In), Boron (B), Aluminium (Al), etc.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is the dopant for tetravalent Si or Ge chosen from the nearby fifth or third group?
cards.back: Si or Ge belongs to the fourth group in the Periodic table and, therefore, we choose the dopant element from nearby fifth or third group, expecting and taking care that the size of the dopant atom is nearly the same as that of Si or Ge.
cards.quote: Si or Ge belongs to the fourth group in the Periodic table and, therefore, we choose the dopant element from nearby fifth or third group, expecting and taking care that the size of the dopant atom is nearly the same as that of Si or Ge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In n-type doping, what happens to the fifth electron of a +5 valency atom in the Si lattice?
cards.back: When an atom of +5 valency element occupies the position of an atom in the crystal lattice of Si, four of its electrons bond with the four silicon neighbours while the fifth remains very weakly bound to its parent atom.
cards.quote: When an atom of +5 valency element occupies the position of an atom in the crystal lattice of Si, four of its electrons bond with the four silicon neighbours while the fifth remains very weakly bound to its parent atom.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What energy frees the extra electron of a donor atom in germanium and in silicon?
cards.back: For example, the energy required is ~ 0.01 eV for germanium, and 0.05 eV for silicon, to separate this electron from its atom.
cards.quote: For example, the energy required is ~ 0.01 eV for germanium, and 0.05 eV for silicon, to separate this electron from its atom.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a donor impurity?
cards.back: Thus, the pentavalent dopant is donating one extra electron for conduction and hence is known as donor impurity.
cards.quote: Thus, the pentavalent dopant is donating one extra electron for conduction and hence is known as donor impurity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the number of electrons from donor atoms depend on the doping level and temperature?
cards.back: The number of electrons made available for conduction by dopant atoms depends strongly upon the doping level and is independent of any increase in ambient temperature.
cards.quote: The number of electrons made available for conduction by dopant atoms depends strongly upon the doping level and is independent of any increase in ambient temperature.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In an n-type semiconductor, why does the number of holes get reduced further?
cards.back: But the rate of recombination of holes would increase due to the increase in the number of electrons. As a result, the number of holes would get reduced further.
cards.quote: But the rate of recombination of holes would increase due to the increase in the number of electrons. As a result, the number of holes would get reduced further.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is an n-type semiconductor? Name its majority and minority carriers.
cards.back: Hence in an extrinsic semiconductor doped with pentavalent impurity, electrons become the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers. These semiconductors are, therefore, known as n-type semiconductors.
cards.quote: Hence in an extrinsic semiconductor doped with pentavalent impurity, electrons become the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers. These semiconductors are, therefore, known as n-type semiconductors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is a p-type semiconductor obtained?
cards.back: This is obtained when Si or Ge is doped with a trivalent impurity like Al, B, In, etc.
cards.quote: This is obtained when Si or Ge is doped with a trivalent impurity like Al, B, In, etc.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In p-type doping, why does the bond with the fourth Si neighbour have a vacancy?
cards.back: The dopant has one valence electron less than Si or Ge and, therefore, this atom can form covalent bonds with neighbouring three Si atoms but does not have any electron to offer to the fourth Si atom. So the bond between the fourth neighbour and the trivalent atom has a vacancy or hole as shown in Fig. 14.8.
cards.quote: The dopant has one valence electron less than Si or Ge and, therefore, this atom can form covalent bonds with neighbouring three Si atoms but does not have any electron to offer to the fourth Si atom. So the bond between the fourth neighbour and the trivalent atom has a vacancy or hole as shown in Fig. 14.8.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Note that the trivalent foreign atom becomes effectively ____ when it shares fourth electron with neighbouring Si atom.
cards.back: Note that the trivalent foreign atom becomes effectively negatively charged when it shares fourth electron with neighbouring Si atom.
cards.quote: Note that the trivalent foreign atom becomes effectively negatively charged when it shares fourth electron with neighbouring Si atom.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How many holes does one acceptor atom give in a p-type semiconductor?
cards.back: It is obvious that one acceptor atom gives one hole.
cards.quote: It is obvious that one acceptor atom gives one hole.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a p-type semiconductor? Name its majority and minority carriers.
cards.back: Thus, for such a material, the holes are the majority carriers and electrons are minority carriers. Therefore, extrinsic semiconductors doped with trivalent impurity are called p-type semiconductors.
cards.quote: Thus, for such a material, the holes are the majority carriers and electrons are minority carriers. Therefore, extrinsic semiconductors doped with trivalent impurity are called p-type semiconductors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why does an extrinsic semiconductor crystal stay overall charge neutral?
cards.back: Note that the crystal maintains an overall charge neutrality as the charge of additional charge carriers is just equal and opposite to that of the ionised cores in the lattice.
cards.quote: Note that the crystal maintains an overall charge neutrality as the charge of additional charge carriers is just equal and opposite to that of the ionised cores in the lattice.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does a dopant reduce the concentration of minority carriers?
cards.back: Hence, the dopant, by adding a large number of current carriers of one type, which become the majority carriers, indirectly helps to reduce the intrinsic concentration of minority carriers.
cards.quote: Hence, the dopant, by adding a large number of current carriers of one type, which become the majority carriers, indirectly helps to reduce the intrinsic concentration of minority carriers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: n-type Si energy bands: where does the donor energy level lie relative to the bottom of the conduction band?
cards.back: the donor energy level ED is slightly below the bottom EC of the conduction band and electrons from this level move into the conduction band with very small supply of energy.
cards.quote: In the energy band diagram of n-type Si semiconductor, the donor energy level ED is slightly below the bottom EC of the conduction band and electrons from this level move into the conduction band with very small supply of energy.

tex.back: the donor energy level $E_D$ is slightly below the bottom $E_{\mathrm{C}}$ of the conduction band and electrons from this level move into the conduction band with very small supply of energy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: p-type Si energy bands: where does the acceptor energy level lie relative to the top of the valence band?
cards.back: the acceptor energy level EA is slightly above the top EV of the valence band
cards.quote: for p-type semiconductor, the acceptor energy level EA is slightly above the top EV of the valence band as shown in Fig. 14.9(b).

tex.back: the acceptor energy level $E_A$ is slightly above the top $E_V$ of the valence band

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: product of the electron and hole concentrations of a semiconductor in thermal equilibrium
cards.back:
The electron and hole concentration in a semiconductor in thermal equilibrium is given by
ne nh = ni2
cards.quote: The electron and hole concentration in a semiconductor in thermal equilibrium is given by ne nh = ni 2 (14.5)

tex.back:
The electron and hole concentration in a semiconductor in thermal equilibrium is given by
$$n_e n_h = n_i^2$$

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Types of extrinsic semiconductors.
cards.back:
n-type
p-type
cards.quote: Such semiconductors are known as extrinsic semiconductors. These are of two types (n-type and p-type).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: n-type vs p-type Si or Ge: the dopant used.
cards.back: n-type semiconducting Si or Ge is obtained by doping with pentavalent atoms (donors) like As, Sb, P, etc., while p-type Si or Ge can be obtained by doping with trivalent atom (acceptors) like B, Al, In etc.
